Take ArguAna: interpolation makes 19.1% of queries worse, the worsened queries drop by 0.213 on average, almost as much as the 0.221 average gain of the improved queries, and the mean net change is only +0.0077. The small rise in the average is the difference left after large gains and large losses across many queries cancel out.

One might suspect that the 0.7 weight was picked on the test data. The authors re-select the weight with leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation: choose α on the other 6 datasets and apply it to the 7th. The resulting deployable tax is 11–25%, slightly higher than with a fixed 0.7, which shows the tax is not caused by tuning on the test set. The risk-sensitive test TRisk works query by query on the nDCG@10 change of fusion relative to dense-only retrieval: gains count as they are, losses are multiplied by (1+α) (the authors use α=5), and the test asks whether this weighted mean is significantly below zero. By this standard, interpolation is significantly riskier than dense-only retrieval on 6 of the 7 datasets, even though its mean score is higher.

3.3 Which quadrant the losses come from

This experiment checks which kind of query the losses come from. The authors split interpolation's per-query gains and losses by the four quadrants of Section 2 (paper Table VII). Result: Sparse-Only queries make up no more than 7% of the total, but 87–95% of them are hurt by fusion, with mean net losses of 0.14 to 0.37 within the quadrant. The reason is that dense retrieval has no relevant document in its top 10 on these queries, and the 0.7 dense weight pushes down the relevant documents BM25 found. Dense-Only queries are the mirror case: BM25 becomes the noise source and 38–65% are hurt. Among Both-Win queries, 10–48% are reordered, with help and harm nearly cancelling and a quadrant net change between −0.04 and +0.01; because this quadrant holds the most queries, it contributes 38–72% of the worsened queries.

These losses come mainly from rank changes, not from relevant documents going missing. Queries whose top-10 recall actually drops are only 1–7%; in most cases the relevant documents are still in the top 10, just moved down a few places. Across all datasets, only 77 queries have all their relevant documents pushed out of the top ten, so the fusion tax is mainly worse ordering, not worse recall.

3.4 A bigger encoder does not remove the tax

This experiment checks whether the fusion tax exists only because the dense model is weak. The authors step the dense encoder up from 22M to 596M, then redo the experiment with BM25 replaced by the learned sparse retriever SPLADE. Result: with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, interpolation still puts 14–43% of queries below the per-query best; with SPLADE it is 14–41% on 6 datasets and 60% on TREC-COVID. A stronger encoder only changes the balance between the two retrievers, and that balance decides which retriever becomes noise on each query, so the share of hurt queries does not decline as the encoder grows.

3.5 Can we tell in advance which queries should not be fused

If this could be predicted, queries could be routed: fuse where fusion helps and use dense-only retrieval elsewhere. This experiment checks whether that is feasible. The authors extract 17 features available at inference time for each query (query length, IDF statistics of its terms, the score gap between the first and second result of each retriever, the overlap of the two top-10 lists, and so on) and train gradient-boosted trees to predict whether fusion will fail. "Failure" means that on this query, fusion's nDCG@10 is more than 0.01 below the better of the two retrievers. Result: AUC is 0.63 within a dataset, falls to 0.59 across datasets, and is as low as 0.49, close to random; 11 of the 17 features flip the direction of their association with failure across datasets. A router built on these features does not beat fixed interpolation on any dataset. A concrete example is the dense side's score lead, the similarity gap between dense retrieval's first and second results: on datasets where dense retrieval is stronger it signals that fusion is safe, but on TREC-COVID it signals that fusion will fail.

3.6 Can reranking repair the damage

This experiment checks whether a cross-encoder reranker after fusion can repair the losses fusion causes. The authors rerank the top 30 with BGE-reranker-v2-m3. After reranking, the reference also becomes reranked dense-only retrieval, and the tax is the share of queries where fusion falls below it. This deployable tax falls by a third only on SciFact, and not at all on FiQA or TREC-COVID, where 16% and 22% of queries still finish below reranked dense-only. The reason is that reranking repairs old losses while creating new ones. Take FiQA: of the 95 queries fusion had hurt, reranking repairs 75, but newly hurts 81, so it gains nothing. After reranking, nDCG@10 barely differs (at most 0.011) whether the candidates come from interpolation or from dense-only retrieval, which means that with a reranker, the fusion step can largely be dropped. The cost is latency: cross-encoder reranking of 30 candidates takes about 1.6 s, while BM25 needs only a few milliseconds per query.

4. Limitations

The authors list five limitations: only retrieval ranking is evaluated, not the final answer generation; only one reranker and one reranking depth are tried; TREC-COVID has only 50 queries, so its percentages fluctuate a lot; latency is measured on one machine only; and the prediction experiment uses only cheap features, without trying LLM judgments.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all 7 datasets are English BEIR datasets whose queries are mostly natural-language questions, and dense retrieval is stronger than BM25 on all 7 of them; in keyword-heavy settings such as e-commerce or code search, Sparse-Only queries may be far more than 7%, and both the quadrant shares and the recommended weight need to be re-measured. Second, Section 3.3 shows that most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; if the downstream system feeds all 10 documents into the generator's context, this loss affects the answer much less, which is exactly the gap left by not evaluating generation.

5. Practical implications

First, before adopting hybrid retrieval, measure the nDCG@10 of each retriever on the target corpus. The authors' advice is that if dense retrieval leads by more than 0.04, use dense-leaning score interpolation (dense weight 0.6–0.7); only when the two are close use RRF, CombMNZ or equal-weight interpolation. This call does not need much labeling; 200–400 queries are enough. The weights also carry over to other datasets: a weight chosen on the other 6 datasets scores at most 0.014 nDCG@10 below the weight tuned directly on that dataset (TREC-COVID is the exception, at 0.031), so there is no need to retune for every corpus.

Second, in online evaluation, report "the share of queries worse than dense-only retrieval" and "the mean loss when worse" alongside the average. These two numbers show directly whether a higher average comes from most queries gaining a little, or from some queries gaining a lot and cancelling out large losses on others.

papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.authors: Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Maximilian Schall, Antoine Chaffin, Sedigheh Eslami, Jonas Golde, De...
papers.summary: Perplexity releases 0.6B and 9B multi-vector retrievers that encode text, images, and document screenshots: each document token stores a 128-d vector, and scoring sums MaxSim of each query vector against document vectors. Both models distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher, ==so they share one vector space== and a 9B offline document index can be queried by a 0.6B online encoder. On 72 domain retrieval tasks the 9B model averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, above 78.0% when both ends use 0.6B. On BrowseComp+ the 9B model lets an agent answer 64.0% correctly with the fewest searches.

deep_reading.content_html:
Perplexity has released two multi-vector retrieval models, pplx-embed-v2-late, at 0.6B and 9B parameters, which encode text, images and screenshots of document pages. They are "late-interaction" retrievers: every document token is stored as a 128-dimensional vector, every query token also gets its own vector, and scoring takes, for each query vector, the largest inner product with any document vector, then sums those maxima (MaxSim). The two models are not trained separately with contrastive learning. Instead both imitate, token by token, the vectors produced by the same 18B teacher, so they land in the same embedding space: a document collection can be indexed offline with the 9B model and queried online with the 0.6B model, scoring directly. On 72 domain retrieval tasks assembled by the authors, the 9B model averages 81.3% nDCG@10, 1.6 points above the runner-up nemotron-3-embed-8b. A 0.6B query against a 9B document index scores 79.6%, 1.6 points above using 0.6B on both sides, at the same query-side cost. This is a short technical report, and the credibility of its main results has to be judged piece by piece. The task list of the domain benchmark is not public, and the labels of the two production benchmarks partly come from Perplexity's own production system; only ViDoRe-V3 and BrowseComp+ can be reproduced independently.

1. Why late interaction, and why distillation

Retrieval models usually trade off between two designs. Single-vector models compress a whole document into one vector, which is fast with approximate nearest-neighbor search but loses detail. Cross-encoders run the query and document through the model together, which works well but needs a separate pass per candidate, so they are only usable for reranking. Late interaction sits in between: document token vectors are computed offline and stored, at query time only the query's vectors are computed, and MaxSim does the scoring. The price is storage, which is why this work compresses each token vector to 128 dimensions.

The authors' other judgment is that small models trained directly with contrastive learning fall short, and fitting the token vectors of a large model works better, especially at small sizes. A by-product is that students of different sizes distilled from the same teacher are interchangeable. The report body, however, gives no numbers comparing distillation with direct contrastive training, so for now this is the authors' experience only.

2. Training pipeline

2.1 The 18B teacher: two-stage contrastive learning

The teacher is Qwen3.5-27B with its last 20 layers pruned, giving 18B, and with the causal mask removed from the attention layers so every token sees both sides of its context. Training has two stages.

The first stage uses query–document pairs. The data come from 28 datasets, further split by language and domain into 981 subsets, 186M pairs in total. 88.3% are text–text, 8.3% text–image and 3.4% text–document-screenshot, and 14M of the text pairs are synthesized by generating queries backward from PDF passages. Sampling weights are adjusted during training to change the three proportions to 56.5%, 30.9% and 12.6%, heavily upsampling images and screenshots. Each batch is drawn from a single subset, so the other documents in the batch (the negatives) are closer to the positive and harder to tell apart. To make subsets appear in their target proportions and at evenly spaced intervals, the authors do not draw independently at each step. They cut 0 to 1 into 981 segments, each as long as its subset's sampling share, with subsets from the same source placed next to each other. At step n they take the fractional part of "random start +n×0.618…" (0.618 being the inverse golden ratio), and the segment it lands in supplies that batch. These points cover 0 to 1 very evenly, so each segment is hit about as often as its length and the hits are spread out in time; subsets from one source form one long segment, so "proportional and evenly spaced" also holds at the source level. The contrastive batch is 16,384 pairs, trained with LoRA (rank 128). In-batch documents whose MaxSim score is within 0.2 of the positive's are not counted as negatives, to reduce false negatives. MaxSim is written as a Triton kernel to avoid materializing the token-level similarity matrix.

The second stage merges the LoRA weights, adds a new rank-32 adapter, freezes the vision part and trains on text triplets only: each query gets one positive and up to 4 hard negatives. Some hard negatives are synthesized by changing key information in highly templated documents, for instance a financial report in a fixed format with a single number changed, which forces the model to read details.

2.2 Students: fitting the teacher's vectors token by token

The student loss is direct. For every valid query and document token, take the Euclidean distance between the student vector and the teacher vector (both L2-normalized), average the query part and the document part separately, and add them. The teacher is not updated.
L=∣Q∣1​(i,t)∈Q∑​∥qitS​−qitT​∥2​+∣D∣1​(i,t)∈D∑​∥ditS​−ditT​∥2​
Because this loss does not rely on in-batch negatives, a batch can mix several subsets, which steadies the gradient. The 9B student is based on Qwen3.5-9B. The authors found LoRA alone could not fit well enough, and they guess that token-level alignment constrains the whole embedding space too tightly. So they fully fine-tune the last 8 layers of the text part and use LoRA elsewhere. The 0.6B student is pruned from Qwen3.5-0.8B, removing 2 of the 3 linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers in each block. It ends up with 594M parameters in total, of which 254M are the token-embedding table and 100M the image encoder, so about 240M are actually active for text. It is fully fine-tuned, because full fine-tuning clearly beat training adapters only on document-screenshot tasks.

3. Experiments

3.1 Text retrieval

The domain benchmark consists of 72 public tasks covering finance, legal, health, conversation, tech and multilingual, with task counts ranging from 4 in tech to 20 in legal. The metric is nDCG@10, averaged with equal weight over the six domains:

The 9B model is best in every domain except health; the 0.6B model is best among sub-1B models in every domain. The 9B model's largest leads are in conversation (+4.1) and tech (+2.9), domains with only 5 and 4 tasks, where a single task's swing moves the average a lot. In legal, the domain with the most tasks, 9B is only 0.5 above nemotron. The authors withhold the task list so that later models cannot tune to it. The reason is understandable, but the cost is that this table cannot be checked.

Q2D-Web is closer to Perplexity's production setting: about 70,000 agent-rewritten production search queries over a corpus of 190M web pages, measured by Recall@1000. Relevant documents have three kinds of labels: documents the agent cited in its answer; documents the production retrieval system ranked high; and the union of those two, extended with documents an LLM judged relevant. The table compares the two pplx models with the strongest baselines:

The second column treats documents ranked high by Perplexity's production retrieval as relevant, which naturally favors models that rank like the production system, and the pplx models lead nemotron most in this column (7.1 points). The authors therefore emphasize the combined labels, which they say reduce this bias. But the first column, "documents cited by the agent", also comes out of the production system's search results and carries the same lean, so none of the three columns is fully neutral. Even so, the 0.6B model beats the 8B nemotron in all three columns, which shows the advantage is not all label bias.

The report also tests the text version of ViDoRe-V3, where document page screenshots are converted to Markdown by OCR before retrieval, again scored by nDCG@10. The 9B model scores 64.7%, the 0.6B 61.2%, and the best baseline, nemotron, 60.6%. This is the only text result that can be reproduced independently.

3.2 Document-screenshot and image retrieval

All three benchmarks below are text-to-image retrieval, scored by nDCG@10 (%).

On images it does not lead across the board. On ViDoRe-V3, EVIE (a vision-only multi-vector model) trained specifically for image retrieval scores higher in both its 8B and 4.5B versions, at 66.4% and 65.9%. But they store 4,096 and 2,048 dimensions per token, while pplx-embed-v2-late stores only 128, so the gap has to be read together with storage cost.

The fairest comparison is topk-embed-v1, also at 128 dimensions: the 0.6B model is 0.4 points above the 2B topk model, while topk at its full 2,048 dimensions is 0.9 points above the 0.6B model. That means under the same storage budget, pplx's small model matches a model of the same kind with more than three times the parameters. On MIRACL-Vision (Wikipedia page screenshots) and PPLX-Q2I (Perplexity's production image-search logs, 10,000 queries and 100,000 images), gemini-embedding-2 scores higher. PPLX-Q2I defines relevant images as "images actually served in production", carrying the same production-system lean as Q2D-Web. EVIE and Nemotron ColEmbed were not evaluated on this set; the authors say their dimensions are too high to make indexing practical.

3.3 Small-model queries + large-model index

Documents are indexed with the 9B model, and queries are encoded with either 9B or 0.6B. A 0.6B query against 9B documents beats 0.6B on both sides in all six domains, raising the average from 78.0% to 79.6%; 9B on both sides scores 81.3%. In other words, switching only the document side recovers almost half of the 9B model's 3.3-point advantage over 0.6B. Query encoding costs the same as pure 0.6B, and the cost of indexing documents is amortized over the life of the index. The report runs this experiment only on the domain benchmark, not on Q2D-Web or the image tasks.

3.4 As the retriever for a search agent

BrowseComp+ has GPT-OSS-120B act as an agent that repeatedly searches a fixed corpus with the retriever under test to answer complex questions, and another LLM grades the answers. The 9B model reaches 64.0% accuracy, 4.9 points above the other late-interaction model, Reason-ModernColBERT, and 8.7 points above the best single-vector model, voyage-4-large. It also needs fewer searches on average than every baseline, and its recall is highest too. A more accurate retriever lets the agent search fewer rounds, a direct cost saving for search agents billed per call.

4. Limitations

The report gives no storage or latency figures, and these are the main cost of late interaction. A rough calculation at the training truncation length: a 1,000-token document stores 128,000 numbers, about 256 KB in half precision. A 1,024-dimensional single vector in half precision takes only 2 KB, about 128 times less. Real systems usually quantize or cluster token vectors; the report does not say what Perplexity does, nor what MaxSim retrieval latency is over 190M web pages. Also, the domain benchmark's task list is not public and cannot be reproduced; the labels of the two production benchmarks lean toward the production system; "distillation beats direct contrastive learning" lacks comparison numbers; and on image retrieval, dedicated vision models and gemini-embedding-2 are still better on some benchmarks.

5. Practical implications

For retrieval teams, the most directly usable idea is "index with the large model, query with the small one": document-side compute is spent once, query-side latency is that of a 0.6B model, and quality is 1.6 points above the small model alone. This requires both models to be distilled from the same teacher; two independently trained models cannot be mixed like this. The 0.6B version has only about 240M active parameters for text, and the authors think it can run on edge devices. If you are evaluating multi-vector retrieval, first measure storage overhead and retrieval latency on your own corpus, and rely mainly on public benchmarks such as ViDoRe-V3. Those are the parts the report either does not answer or that cannot be verified.

papers.title: OpenSaC: A Python Library for Search as Code in Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Qi Liu, Jiaxin Mao, Fengbin Zhu, Tat-Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.summary: OpenSaC lets research agents write programs that combine search, reading, reranking, and local processing, returning selected evidence to the model. On BrowseComp, it cuts model-token use by 37.8%.
papers.key_insight: Process intermediate evidence in code and preserve source links for reuse. The library reduces repeated model reading, but requires an execution environment. WideSearch row F1 falls slightly, so efficiency gains do not guarantee better answers.

papers.title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Zijun Dou, Kun Luo, Chaofan Li, Shuqi Lu, Zheng Liu
papers.summary: Deep search can reinforce an early mistaken hypothesis. FALCA separates answer proposals from independent counterevidence searches and trains research-state revision with hierarchical credit. Its 4B model reaches 56.0% accuracy on BrowseComp.
papers.key_insight: Give counterevidence checking its own context. A useful falsification report names conflicting evidence and unmet constraints, giving the next search a specific gap to resolve.

papers.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
papers.authors: Yan, Liang, Anuj Agarwal, Aditya Reddy Cheruku
papers.summary: In Adobe Express's AI assistant, retrieval metrics that assume the user saw a ranked list and acted on it stop working. The chat entry point has a reformulation rate of 44.4%, higher than the template gallery search served by the same retrieval system, at 33.1%. The reason is that reformulation means different things on the two sides. In the gallery, a user reformulates because the results were irrelevant and they try other words. In chat, most reformulations come after the user sees a generated result and wants to tweak it. More surprising still, the assistant actually called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts. The paper's evaluation framework measures in three layers: it scores the returned results against relevance labels when retrieval fires, then checks whether the returned assets were used, and finally whether the user exported. Four log fields record the retrieval ID, the full returned list, which asset each action used, and which retrieval that asset came from, linking every use and export back to that retrieval.

deep_reading.content_html:
Adobe Express's template gallery search and its AI assistant run on the same retrieval system and serve the same users. Intuition says assistant users don't look at result lists, so they should reformulate queries less. In fact the chat entry point has a reformulation rate of 44.4%, against 33.1% for the gallery, 11 points higher. The reason is that "reformulation" means different things on the two sides. In the gallery, a user reformulates because the results were irrelevant and they try other words. In chat, most reformulations come after the user sees a generated result and wants to tweak it, such as "a bit bluer" or "use a bolder font". More surprising still, the assistant actually called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts. The three Adobe authors call this the attribution gap: CTR, MRR and behavioral NDCG all assume the user saw a ranked list and acted on it, and in an AI assistant that assumption breaks in three directions at once. The paper's evaluation framework, LARA, uses three independent layers of measurement plus four log fields to give credit back to retrieval, without training any new model.

1. The problem: the agent reads first, the user comes later

The authors argue that the failure comes from three structural changes, none of which tuning can fix.

The first change is who looks at the results. In the gallery, a user searches "birthday invitation", scrolls through 40 templates and clicks one, and that click is a grade for retrieval. In the assistant, the user says they want a birthday invitation, a search sub-agent retrieves templates, and the agent picks one and turns it straight into a design; the user never sees the other 39. There may be no click at all, and what the user does see has already been filtered and reordered by the agent.

The second change is that action takes longer to arrive. The same asset may be retrieved in turn 1 and again in turn 3, and only exported in turn 5 or even in another session. The logs have no identifier linking that export to a particular retrieval, so timing alone cannot tell which retrieval deserves the credit.

The third change is that nobody can say what caused the outcome. When the result is bad, there is no way to tell whether retrieval or generation went wrong. When the result is good, the model may have quietly made up for a failed retrieval.

Without per-component instrumentation, teams can only watch session-level signals such as retries, abandonment and task completion. The authors point out that retries alone go wrong in both directions. They fire when generation fails for reasons that have nothing to do with retrieval, and they stay silent when the model covers for retrieval. The second failure is harder to catch: retrieval went wrong but the model filled in the answer itself, the user did not retry, and in session-level signals it looks exactly like real success.

2. Method: measure where a problem is first visible

LARA's principle is to measure each component's failures at the earliest point where they can be seen. So it has three layers; the higher the layer, the closer it is to product outcomes and the more it depends on the lineage fields described later.

Layer 1 asks only about retrieval itself: did the sub-agent return the right assets in the right order? The metrics are null rate, precision@1, precision@K and NDCG@K, computed at the moment retrieval fires from server-side logs with offline relevance labels (human or LLM judge), independent of what the user or agent does afterwards. CTR serves here only as a secondary directional signal. Only this layer can catch a retrieval failure that the model has masked.

Layer 2 asks whether what came back was actually used, and whether there are signs that retrieval was wrong. This layer counts positive evidence and failure evidence separately and reports them by "retrieval role". The retrieval role is written to the log at retrieval time and says what the retrieval was for: finding something directly, finding something to look at, finding something to act on, serving as a reference input for generation, being one step in a larger task, or depending on context. The layer has four metrics:

  • Genuine positive rate (GPR): the share of retrievals where, after the results were shown to the user, the user actively used a returned asset, for example by asking a follow-up about it, or by selecting, editing or exporting it.
  • Agent consumption rate (ACR): the share of retrievals where the agent used a returned asset within the same request, before the user received anything, for example when a user asks in one sentence for a logo with the background removed. This also counts as positive evidence, but it is tracked separately, because it reflects only the agent's judgment; the user's later action is the independent confirmation.
  • Observable retrieval failure rate (ORF): the share of retrievals followed by one of three retrieval-specific signals. The first is the user saying the retrieved object or path is wrong. The second is searching again for the same unresolved need. The third is the agent using something else when the flow should have used the returned asset. When the user keeps the asset and only modifies the edit or the generated result, that is a "downstream correction" and does not count as a retrieval failure. 1−ORF should be reported alongside GPR and ACR, but it must not be treated as satisfaction.
  • Unobserved outcome rate (UOR): the share of retrievals with neither evidence of use nor a failure signal. It is its own category, counted as neither abandonment nor success.

Layer 3 asks whether the user reached their goal. In a creative tool the clearest signals are export, share and download. Task completion is defined per retrieval role, and whether the goal was reached needs an LLM judge or human labels. Only when these success events can be linked back, through the lineage fields, to the retrieval that supplied the asset does this layer become a signal about retrieval; otherwise it only reflects overall product health.

3. Read two layers together, then add four log fields

Reading Layer 1 and Layer 2 side by side tells you which component went wrong:

Layer 1Layer 2Diagnosis
LowHigh ORFRetrieval returned the wrong assets
HighLow ORF, many downstream correctionsAssets were fine; generation failed
HighHigh ORF (agent rejection)The agent skipped good results and used content the model generated or remembered itself
LowORF near zeroA silent retrieval failure masked by the model

The last row is the most dangerous. Without Layer 1 this failure is completely invisible; with Layer 1 it shows up the moment retrieval fires, with no need to wait for user complaints to pile up.

For Layers 2 and 3 to work, the logs must be able to link actions back to retrievals. Today Adobe's production logs have no field shared by retrieval events and action events, and the authors propose four fields to close the gap. The first is a unique retrieval_id on every retrieval. The second is returned_asset_ids, the full ranked list at the moment retrieval fires, recorded before the generation layer filters or reorders it; this field alone makes Layer 1 computable, so it is the single change with the best payoff. The third is a consumed_asset_id on every action event, whether the action comes from the user or from an agent tool call. The fourth is a source_retrieval_id on the same event, pointing to the retrieval that supplied the asset; for an asset already placed in the document, the field is inherited from the placement event.

All four are additions to logging, not predictive models. source_retrieval_id sits on the action event and holds the retrieval that actually supplied the asset; once the asset is placed in the document, later actions inherit the value recorded at placement. Because it points to a retrieval rather than a session, attribution stays clear even when the same asset is retrieved again over several turns or exported in a new session. Together the four fields can also recover the rank of the asset that was actually used within the retrieval results, independent of the order finally shown to the user. That lets RAG evaluation frameworks such as RAGAs and ARES use direct attribution instead of guessing from timing.

One example ties the four fields together. A user says in chat, "Find a birthday invitation template and change the title to Xiaoming's 6th birthday." The retrieval event records retrieval_id=r1 and 20 candidates. The agent picks the fourth one and changes the title; this is an agent event carrying consumed_asset_id and source_retrieval_id=r1, and it counts toward ACR. Two days later the user exports from the editor, and the export event inherits r1, counting as a "retrieval-attributed export" in Layer 3. Without these fields, the export would land in another session and the original chat session would be counted as abandoned.

4. Production data from Adobe Express

The authors analyzed production sessions from August 2026. LARA's lineage fields are not live yet, so every "was it used" number below is inferred from timing. Session, user and query counts are withheld under Adobe's disclosure policy; the paper says only that gallery volume is roughly 8–9 times the assistant's.

The data confirms the points from Section 1 in three ways. The first is that the agent reads first. The assistant's CTR is close to zero when every conversation is counted. But 99.7% of interactions never called retrieval and never showed a single result, so they do not belong in a CTR denominator at all; counting them drives CTR toward zero. When retrieval does fire, it behaves normally: the null rate is 1.51%, and users click about 1.05 times per returned result grid. Testing directly whether the agent used the results would need ACR, which cannot be computed yet.

The second is delayed action. Assistant sessions overall (chat and in-editor entry points combined) average 2.04 prompts, and chat-entry sessions alone average 2.65, with the same asset reappearing in later turns. An export started from chat is logged under a different session_guid once the user leaves the chat interface. Session-level attribution then counts those users as abandoning, so the chat abandonment rate (59.5%) is overstated and engagement is understated.

The third is that retrieval and generation are mixed together. The reformulation inversion from the opening is the example: one behavioral signal mixes retrieval failures with tweaks to generated results, so the aggregate number says nothing. LARA splits it in two: "search reformulation", counted only on retrieval turns, and "downstream correction", counted on the other turns.

With current logs, the team can compute only the null rate and clicks per grid today. Precision@K and NDCG@K also need returned_asset_ids and a labeled sample. GPR, ACR, ORF and UOR need the other three fields plus the retrieval role, and for now can only be obtained by labeling traces by hand. In other words, the team can confirm that retrieval works when it fires, but cannot yet confirm whether the user or the agent actually used what came back.

5. A surprise: retrieval is almost never called

Gallery search is retrieval by definition, while the assistant called retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts; about 82% of assistant activity is generative editing with no corresponding search scenario at all. The authors think the bigger risk may be missed retrieval: the planner routes "help me find a birthday invitation template" to generative editing, no retrieval event is created, and Layer 1 has nothing to score. In Table 3's "prompts with retrieval" row, 0.31% is the share of prompts across the whole assistant that actually triggered retrieval; the chat-entry column shows 10.7%, which the paper marks as only directional without saying how it was counted. If the 10.7% reflects the share of prompts where users wanted retrieval, the gap between it and 0.31% is a first rough estimate of missed retrieval. The two cover different scopes (chat entry only versus the whole assistant), so it can only be rough.

The authors call planner routing Layer 0 and treat it as an extension of LARA rather than a fourth layer. It has two metrics. The misroute rate is the share of retrieval calls whose prompt was not actually in scope for retrieval; those calls should be removed from Layer 1. The missed-retrieval rate is the share of prompts with retrieval intent that did not trigger retrieval, which needs ground-truth intent labels. In a sample of 273 prompts, about 5–7% contained two or more distinct retrieval intents, so routing also has to be able to split multi-intent requests.

6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list are concrete. All the evidence comes from one deployment, and the 0.31% figure and the reformulation inversion may be specific to a creative assistant dominated by generative editing. None of the lineage fields is live, so every Layer 2 number is inferred from timing, and the retrieval roles were inferred after the fact rather than recorded at retrieval time. The chat abandonment rate is overstated by cross-session exports. The data was not validated for schema or value ranges, and synthetic traffic was removed by hand. Latency and tokens per successful task were not instrumented by stage either. LARA covers only the retrieval component; how the agent understands intent, generates queries and splits multi-intent requests needs separate instrumentation. This is a short industry paper, and the framework has not been validated across multiple deployments or in online experiments.

The authors' three lessons for practitioners are useful. First, do not use the assistant's overall CTR or reformulation rate as retrieval metrics: retrieval metrics should be counted only on turns where retrieval fired, and reformulations should be split into search reformulations and downstream corrections. Second, start by logging the full ranked list when retrieval fires; only this field makes Layer 1 computable. Third, define "the user actively used it" once and publish the definition: in Express chat, the effective action rate (the share of responses after which the user does something meaningful with the result) ranges from 7.6% to 40.5% depending on which behaviors are counted. Countable behaviors include continuing with the result in a follow-up prompt, selecting, editing and exporting; the paper gives only the two endpoints, without listing which behaviors each includes or stating the denominator. Without a shared definition the numbers cannot be compared. For teams embedding search into an agent, the paper's biggest reminder is that when retrieval is called on only 0.31% of prompts, the question is not only whether it ranks well, but whether it gets called at all.

papers.title: Chunk Recomputation under Real Document Revisions: Measuring Update Cost and Retrieval Quality of Fixed, Recursive, and Content-Defined Chunking
papers.authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
papers.summary: Chunking schemes for RAG are almost always compared on one static corpus, yet the documents in a knowledge base keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so if an edit moves a chunk boundary, the chunks on either side become new embedding inputs even when not a single word in them changed. The authors take adjacent revisions of Chinese and English Wikipedia articles and allow an old vector to be reused only when a chunk's complete embedding input is byte-identical to one in the old version. They compare three chunking methods: non-overlapping fixed-size chunking, paragraph-first recursive chunking and content-defined chunking, which hashes a sliding window of a few words and cuts wherever the hash meets a preset condition. Fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, yet the three methods differ in evidence recall by less than 2 percentage points within each language. Fixed-size chunking shifts everything after the insertion point, so none of the downstream windows can match the old version, which is why it recomputes the most.

deep_reading.content_html:
Chunking schemes for RAG are almost always compared on one static corpus, yet the documents in a knowledge base keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so if an edit moves a chunk boundary, the chunks on either side become new embedding inputs even when not a single word in them changed. This 6-page short paper measures that update cost directly: the authors take 120 pairs of adjacent revisions of Chinese and English Wikipedia articles, allow an old vector to be reused only when a chunk's complete embedding input is byte-identical to one in the old version, and compare three chunking methods with a frozen BGE-M3 encoder. On the 116 articles where all three methods succeed, non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC) 43–54%; under a 2048-token retrieval budget, the three differ in evidence recall by less than 2 percentage points within each language. Fixed-size chunking shifts everything after the insertion point, so none of the downstream windows can match the old version, which is why it recomputes the most. Which of recursive chunking and CDC is cheaper flips as the chunk-length parameters change.

1. Why measure update cost

An English article had only 0.13% of its text edited, yet fixed-size chunking recomputed 49% of its embedding input while paragraph-first chunking recomputed only 8%. This example from the paper's dataset shows that the amount edited and the amount recomputed can be far apart, and the gap is determined by the chunking rule.

For a knowledge base that is continually updated, the amount recomputed maps directly to embedding compute and to writes into the vector index. Earlier chunking evaluations only compared retrieval quality, but two schemes with similar retrieval quality can differ a lot in update cost: on the English articles in this paper, fixed-size chunking's mean recompute fraction is 1.5 times that of paragraph-first chunking (57% vs 38%). The authors want to answer three questions: how much each of the three chunking methods must recompute; whether that amount is driven by edit size, edit position or cut-point rules; and whether the scheme that recomputes less also retrieves worse.

2. Measurement

The reuse rule is strict: a chunk's complete embedding input (its text plus the encoder's special tokens) must be byte-identical to the input of some chunk in the old version for the old vector to be reused; a single differing character makes it a new input. The cache holds only the previous version of the same document and does not match across documents. The recompute fraction is defined as:
Rc​=∑x∈Uc​(Dnew​)​T(x)∑x∈Mc​​T(x)​
Here Uc​(Dnew​) is the set of distinct embedding inputs that chunking method c produces on the new version, Mc​ is the part of it not found in the old version's cache, and $T(x)$ is the number of input tokens of chunk x. Rc​=0 means everything is reused and Rc​=1 means everything is recomputed. The authors also run a no-edit control: chunking the same version twice must give Rc​=0, otherwise it counts as a pipeline failure.

All three chunking methods see only the current version and fixed parameters, never how the old version was chunked:

  • Fixed-size chunking: greedily cuts non-overlapping windows of at most 304 tokens.
  • Recursive chunking: splits any span longer than the 400-token target, preferring blank lines, then line breaks, then sentence-ending punctuation (Latin or full-width) followed by whitespace, and falls back to fixed windows only when none works; it then greedily packs the small units up to the target length.
  • CDC: uses the Steadlith implementation, which computes Rabin rolling fingerprints over the word sequence (a hash of the few words in a sliding window). Its cut rule: once a chunk reaches 176 tokens, it cuts at the first position whose hash has its low 8 bits all zero (Steadlith's default); if none appears by 352 tokens, it falls back to the last position whose low 6 bits are all zero, and failing that cuts at 352 tokens. The method was originally built for file-system deduplication; cut points depend only on nearby content, so inserting bytes near the front of a file does not move the cut points after it.

The chunk-length parameters of the three methods were tuned in advance so that their median chunk lengths are close (the actual maximum ratio is 1.17).

Retrieval quality is measured as follows: each article has two questions, 240 in total, and annotators mark on each version the character spans that answer the question. At retrieval time the candidate pool holds all articles collected in the same batch (the paper does not give the batch size): the article being asked about appears in the version under test, the others in their old version. Chunks are ranked by dot product, and whole chunks are packed into a 2048-token budget in rank order; recall is 1 if the packed chunks cover one complete evidence set.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main result: fixed-size chunking recomputes the most, recall differs little

This experiment answers how much each method must recompute and whether retrieval quality differs. The authors average the recompute fraction and evidence recall with fixed parameters over the 116 articles where all three methods succeed (paper Table I):

LanguageChunkingRecompute fractionEvidence recallMedian chunk length (tokens)
ChineseFixed-size68.4%97.4%304
ChineseRecursive55.7%98.3%356
ChineseCDC54.0%98.3%314
EnglishFixed-size57.4%96.7%304
EnglishRecursive37.9%96.8%342
EnglishCDC42.8%95.0%291

Paired by article, recursive chunking recomputes 12.7 percentage points less than fixed-size chunking (Chinese, 95% interval −19.7 to −6.2) and 19.6 points less (English); CDC recomputes 14.4 and 14.7 points less than fixed-size chunking. Paired differences in recall range from −1.9 to +0.9 points, with all intervals including or touching 0. The authors state explicitly that these intervals cannot rule out a drop in recall and do not prove equivalence, so they do not rank the methods by recall.

Recursive chunking's advantage is smaller in Chinese than in English because of its cut-point rules: Chinese sentence-ending punctuation is usually not followed by a space, so overly long Chinese paragraphs cannot be cut at sentence boundaries and fall back to fixed windows.

The smaller the edit, the larger the gap. On English articles with less than 5% edited, fixed-size chunking recomputes 46% of its embedding input on average, while recursive chunking and CDC need only about a quarter, because their cut points follow the content and an edit does not shift every later cut point. The Chinese articles follow the same pattern: fixed-size chunking recomputes over 60%, and CDC the least (36%). When more than half is edited, all three methods must recompute 60–90%, and at that point the choice of chunking no longer matters.

3.2 Edit position: why fixed-size chunking recomputes so much

This experiment tests whether "boundary shift" is the main source of recomputation. It changes only one variable: the same 1% insertion is placed at the start, middle or end of the article, with everything else unchanged. Result: fixed-size chunking falls from 100% for an insertion at the start to about 12% for one at the end, because every window after the insertion point moves back by the length of the insertion and no downstream chunk can be reused. Recursive chunking and CDC stay below 30% at all three positions, as paragraph breaks and content-fingerprint cut points realign quickly after the edit.

The authors also run a verbatim check: how much of the recomputed input is text that already exists unchanged in the old version. On English articles, 50% of the tokens fixed-size chunking recomputes are text present verbatim in the old version, 33% for CDC and 12% for recursive chunking (47%, 45% and 37% in Chinese). This text was not changed at all; it was only cut into different chunks, so recomputing it is caused entirely by the cut-point rule.

3.3 Whether recursive chunking or CDC is cheaper depends on parameters

This experiment checks whether the ranking of the two content-aware methods is stable. Without retuning, the authors try 6 target chunk lengths between 256 and 496 tokens for each method (for CDC, the maximum length) and compare paired settings whose median-length ratio is at most 1.15. Result: the CDC-minus-recursive recompute difference ranges from −2.4 to +6.2 points in English and from −0.7 to +5.5 in Chinese, flipping sign in both languages. For example, in English raising recursive chunking's target length from 400 to 448 raises its recompute fraction from 37.9% to 46.2%, while CDC at the same 448 is 43.8%. The reason is that recursive chunking packs several small paragraphs into one chunk; once an edit changes one paragraph's length, the packing of several following paragraphs can change too, and the larger the target length, the farther this chain reaction propagates. Fixed-size chunking recomputes the most in every setting.

The authors checked the cost once more on the arXivEdits paper-revision data: the mean recompute fractions of fixed-size, recursive and CDC chunking are 94.5%, 81.4% and 80.2%, with fixed-size still highest. The text-extraction noise of this dataset is unquantified, so it serves only as side evidence on cost.

3.4 Overlapping windows are not the fix

A common remedy is to let adjacent fixed windows overlap by 32 or 64 tokens. The result is a recompute fraction within 1.3 points of the non-overlapping version, 10–26% more total embedding input, and English recall down by 3.0 and 3.9 points, because the duplicated text uses up the 2048-token retrieval budget.

4. Limitations

The authors list these limitations. Wikipedia is the only source. The annotations of the 240 questions were not independently adjudicated by multiple people. The revision pairs were collected in three rounds (the first two inspected by hand, the larger third filtered automatically and checked twice by a model). When an author re-checked a stratified sample of 60 labels from the second and third rounds, 57 matched the original annotation, and the 3 mismatches were all questions labeled unanswerable whose versions actually contained relevant information. The median chunk-length ratio of the three methods is 1.17, above the preset 1.15; only one encoder is used; and the related method KARA was not run. KARA keeps the previous version's chunk layout, builds a graph over candidate cut points and picks the shortest path that reuses the most old chunks; it is built for incremental updates, so without it we do not know how much further such methods could cut recomputation. CDC failed on 4 Chinese articles because CDC splits words on spaces, so a long run of Chinese text without spaces is treated as a single unit of 403–550 tokens, exceeding the 352 maximum.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all three methods recovered all the evidence in 105 of the 116 articles, and recall is generally above 95%, close to the ceiling, so this retrieval setup cannot distinguish small quality differences between methods. Second, the recompute fraction measures embedding input and is not converted into latency or cost; if embedding is a small part of the whole update pipeline, for example when index rebuilding or review costs more, a gap of a few tens of percentage points is diluted in the total cost.

5. Practical implications

First, if a knowledge base is edited often and in small amounts, do not use non-overlapping fixed-size chunking. Switching to paragraph-first recursive chunking takes the mean recompute fraction on English articles from 57% to 38%, and from 46% to 25% on small-edit articles, with retrieval recall essentially unchanged. The precondition is to use the byte-identical input as the cache key, so that vectors are reused whenever the text has not changed.

Second, when evaluating chunking schemes, report the recompute fraction together with retrieval quality, and measure both under your own chunk-length parameters. The ranking of recursive chunking and CDC flips with parameters, so no ranking in the paper can be carried over as is. For Chinese corpora, check whether the cut-point rules rely on spaces; otherwise recursive chunking falls back to fixed windows and CDC fails outright.

papers.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Sijia Luo, Mengjie Gao, Yuxiao He, Mengshu Sun, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
papers.summary: EG-GRPO rewards the first search step that finds support for a required claim, then compares actions from similar evidence states. The 4B agent reaches 45.9% accuracy on GAIA.
papers.key_insight: Reward newly acquired evidence rather than repeated citations. Conditioning comparisons on what an agent already knows reduces unfair comparisons between early and nearly finished trajectories; fallback grouping handles sparse state matches.

papers.title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents
papers.authors: Qirui Liu, Hao Chen, Yi Wen, Weijie Shi, Yao Zhao, Xianhe Chen, Hao Zhao, Xing Tang, Weihong Luo, Yuyu Luo
papers.summary: A search agent can answer correctly without using retrieved evidence. Grounded Credit Assignment separates credit for finding evidence from credit for answering. On the larger evaluated model, it improves average exact match over Search-R1 by 6.3 percentage points.
papers.key_insight: Reward evidence acquisition separately from answer correctness. Otherwise, a lucky answer from memory credits the entire retrieval trace and can improve accuracy while weakening grounding. The proposed correction uses verifiable sub-outcomes without an extra reward model.

papers.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Yiteng Tu, Qingyi Pan, Weihang Su, Jiaxin Mao, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
papers.summary: When rewriting a query vector with first-round retrieved documents or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE), the usual approach averages feedback vectors and interpolates with the original query. DIFF argues that ==each piece of feedback only supports correcting the query along one direction, so other directions should not be pulled back by it==: it subtracts the component parallel to the original query to get each feedback's rotation direction and magnitude, constrains only the projection of the correction onto that direction, weights by query–feedback similarity and group agreement, and solves a K×K linear system—without training any model. On 14 BEIR subsets, bge-base with HyDE rises from 0.5492 to 0.5717 mean NDCG@10; with retrieved-document feedback, vector averaging falls to 0.5045 while DIFF scores 0.5522.

deep_reading.content_html:
In dense retrieval, short queries often under-specify what the user wants. A common fix is to obtain some "feedback" text first, such as the top documents from a first retrieval pass or a hypothetical answer written by an LLM (HyDE), and use it to modify the query vector. Most existing methods average the feedback vectors or interpolate them with the original query. That treats every feedback item as "what the new query should look like" and pulls the query toward it as a whole. This Tsinghua paper proposes DIFF (Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion) and argues that this causes interference: a feedback item usually supports a correction along one direction only, yet it also pulls the query back along every direction it says nothing about. DIFF first computes the direction each feedback item adds relative to the original query and requires the corrected query to agree with the feedback only along that direction, leaving other directions free. It then weights each constraint by feedback quality and adds a "don't move too far from the original query" term as a safeguard. The whole procedure has a closed-form solution and trains no model. On 14 BEIR subsets, 3 retrievers and 4 feedback sources, DIFF has the highest average NDCG@10 in all 12 settings. But with first-pass retrieved documents as feedback it barely improves on the original query without feedback. With LLM-generated feedback, its lead over the strongest baseline, AnchorQE, is about as large as the swing from hyperparameter choice. So the paper's more reliable contribution is "not being dragged down by noisy feedback", not "significantly better retrieval".

1. The problem: treating feedback as target points loses complementary information

Let the original query vector be q, and let feedback item i propose a correction ei​=ℓi​ui​ relative to q, where ui​ is a direction (unit vector) and ℓi​ a magnitude. Pointwise fitting wants the correction δ to be close to ei​, i.e. it minimizes ∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2. The authors split this into two terms:
∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2=(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2+∥(I−ui​ui⊤​)δ∥2
The first term asks δ's component along ui​ to equal ℓi​, which is what we want. The second penalizes δ's components along all other directions, which may be exactly the corrections other feedback items support. For example, take the query "Apple launch event": one feedback document is about a new phone, another about a new computer. Pointwise fitting pulls the query to the middle, going only halfway in each direction.

The authors prove in the appendix that with equal weights, the correction from directional constraints is never smaller than from pointwise fitting, with equality only when all feedback directions are collinear. The difference is largest when the feedback directions are mutually orthogonal. Under directional constraints the correction along direction j is τj​ℓj​/(λ+τj​); under pointwise fitting the denominator also adds the sum of every other item's weight, so the correction is diluted by the other feedback. The proof shows that directional constraints "move further", but moving further is not the same as moving correctly; that has to be tested by experiment.

2. Method: four steps

The first step computes each feedback item's new direction. All vectors are L2-normalized and lie on the unit sphere. For a feedback vector fi​, compute its similarity to the query si​=q⊤fi​, then remove the part parallel to the query to get ri​=fi​−si​q. The direction ui​ of ri​ is where this feedback wants to rotate the query, and its length ℓi​ equals the sine of the angle between them, measuring how much the feedback brings that the original query lacks. The authors deliberately separate "how much is new" (ℓi​) from "how trustworthy" (decided by si​), so that "very different from the query" is not mistaken for "informative and trustworthy".

The second step scores each feedback item's confidence. Confidence τi​=g⋅ai​ has two levels. Item quality ai​: the si​ of all feedback for the same query are standardized by their median and median absolute deviation, then passed through a sigmoid. Feedback closer to the query gets more weight, and the score does not depend on the absolute similarity scale of a given model. Set confidence g: compute the mean μ of all correction vectors, let S=∥μ∥2 be the strength of the mean direction and V the average squared distance of each correction vector from μ (the spread); the geometric confidence is ggeo​=S/(S+V/K), with K the number of feedback items, between 0 and 1. g is high when the feedback agrees on a direction and low when it points every which way. It is finally multiplied by the set's average item quality, because a set of uniformly weak feedback can still agree with itself.

The third step solves for the correction jointly. The objective keeps only each feedback item's constraint along its own direction, plus a penalty on the size of the correction:
δ∗=argδmin​ 2λ​∥δ∥2+21​i∑​τi​(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2
This has a closed-form solution requiring only a K×K linear system (K is the number of feedback items, 5 in the main experiments), at a cost of O(K2D+K3) where D is the embedding dimension.

The fourth step maps the correction back to the sphere: the final rotation angle is the smaller of ∥δ∗∥ and "g × the maximum allowed angle θup​", and q′=cosϕq+sinϕδ∗/∥δ∗∥. When the feedback set is untrustworthy, g is small and the query barely moves.

3. Experiments

Setup: 14 BEIR subsets (including argument retrieval ArguAna, fact checking FEVER, multi-hop QA HotpotQA, MSMARCO, Google search questions NQ (Natural Questions), scientific claim verification SciFact, pandemic literature search TREC-COVID and others), and three retrievers: bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2 and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. There are two kinds of feedback: the top K documents from first-pass retrieval (PRF), and three kinds of text generated by Qwen3.8-27B (HyDE hypothetical documents, Q2D query expansion, CoT reasoning). All methods share the same encoder, feedback and index; only the fusion method differs. Baselines include vector averaging (VPRF), concatenate-then-re-encode (Concat-P/L), OR-PRF which keeps only orthogonal components, DIME (per-dimension importance selection) and its refinement Eclipse, and AnchorQE, which needs extra retrieval to estimate weights.

3.1 Main results

The table gives average NDCG@10 over the 14 subsets; the original query's score without feedback is in parentheses:

Two things stand out. First, with retrieved documents as feedback, plain averaging drags the score below the original query, from 0.5492 to 0.5045 on BGE; in this column DIFF merely avoids losing points. The paper's own significance marks agree: on E5 and Qwen, DIFF's change relative to the original query is not significant, and only BGE's +0.003 is marked significant. Second, with LLM-generated feedback every method improves, and DIFF is very close to AnchorQE. On E5 + HyDE the gap is 0.0002 and with CoT feedback on BGE it is 0.0004, and the paper marks no significant difference in either cell. AnchorQE needs extra retrieval to estimate weights and DIFF does not; that is DIFF's practical advantage when the scores tie.

3.2 Per-query changes beneath the average

This figure explains why the PRF average barely moves. VPRF makes many queries clearly worse, with a batch losing 0.4 to 0.6. DIFF leaves the vast majority of queries essentially unchanged, with roughly as many getting better as worse. The reason is that retrieved documents point in scattered directions, so set confidence g is low and step four squeezes the rotation angle to almost nothing. In other words, DIFF's behavior under noisy feedback is close to "don't move". That is robust, but it also means DIFF fails to pick out the useful few among the retrieved documents. The authors report that under HyDE feedback DIFF improves clearly more queries than it hurts, while still leaving many queries unchanged.

The appendix gives per-subset results on BGE. The table picks the subsets with the most visible changes:

Under HyDE the gains come mainly from QA and entity-retrieval tasks such as NQ, TREC-COVID and DBPedia, because the LLM's hypothetical answers resemble the target documents in style. Quora is duplicate-question retrieval, where a hypothetical answer does not match the target's genre, and DIFF ends up slightly below the original query. Subset by subset, under HyDE DIFF beats AnchorQE on 10 subsets and loses on 4.

3.4 Ablations

On BGE, one component is removed or replaced at a time:
