Reverting to pointwise fitting is among the largest drops, which supports the paper's central claim. Under PRF, though, every variant in the table falls below the original query's 0.5492, and only full DIFF is above it, by 0.003. So the components mainly bring the loss down to zero rather than producing a gain. Under HyDE, removing item quality drops the score from 0.5717 to 0.5481, showing that generated hypothetical documents vary in quality and must be treated differently.

3.5 Hyperparameters and efficiency

DIFF has two hyperparameters: the pull back toward the original query λ and the maximum rotation angle θup​, searched on a 3×3 grid. Under PRF the 9 results range from 0.5452 to 0.5522, only 5 of them above the original query. The best setting uses the small angle π/12, which again says the best strategy with retrieved feedback is to barely move. Under HyDE the 9 results range from 0.5631 to 0.5717, and only 2 beat AnchorQE's 0.5700. The paper does not say which data the grid search used. If settings were picked directly on the test set, DIFF's lead over AnchorQE lies within this range of variation.

On efficiency, timed on 10 queries, DIFF takes 0.258 seconds, on par with vector averaging at 0.247 seconds, while AnchorQE takes 3.67 times as long as DIFF because of its extra retrieval. But 10 queries is a tiny sample, good only for the order of magnitude.

4. Limitations

The main one is in the main table and the distribution plot: with first-pass retrieved documents as feedback, DIFF gains almost nothing over the original query; its value is "not being dragged down by noise". Next, the lead over AnchorQE with generated feedback is small and may depend on hyperparameter choice, and the paper reports no variance across runs. Also, experiments are only on BEIR, the largest retriever is 0.6B, and there is no validation on production-scale corpora or larger embedding models. Generated feedback also comes from a single LLM.

5. Practical implications

If your system already uses HyDE or query expansion and averages the encoded generated text with the original query, consider switching to DIFF. It relies only on the vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and adds one 5×5 linear solve per query, matching AnchorQE without extra retrieval calls. Before rollout, evaluate separately by query type: for tasks like Quora's "find similar questions", a hypothetical answer is the wrong kind of text to begin with. If your feedback comes from first-pass retrieval results, this paper suggests the gain is limited. Treat DIFF as insurance against averaging dragging your metrics down, not as a source of improvement.

papers.title: Let Agents Design How They Search: Automatic Interface Optimization for Agentic Search
papers.authors: Sangjune An, Jaeyoon Jung, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Hae Beom Lee
papers.summary: Korea University and KAIST have Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) design retrieval tools for a search agent: it reads each question's execution log and score, jointly edits pre-generated index files, executable search scripts, and usage instructions, and after 10 rounds keeps the best version on the optimization set. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 on four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0. Prompt-only optimization reaches 75.6% and 52.0, ==so the rest of the gain comes from the generated index files and search scripts==; handing the interface unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite still beats DCI (73.9% vs 60.9%).

deep_reading.content_html:
When an LLM agent searches a document collection, the tools it can use, how the collection is pre-organized, and how the prompt teaches it to use those tools together make up its "search interface". Today's interfaces are hand-designed and generic across collections; DCI (direct corpus interaction), for example, simply gives the agent a terminal and lets it read raw documents with commands like grep and cat. SearchWeaver, from Korea University and KAIST, instead has a coding agent (Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5) design the interface. It reads the search agent's full execution logs and per-question scores, works out why searches failed, and revises three things at once: pre-built index files, executable search scripts, and usage instructions for the search agent. It then reruns the agent and checks the score, for 10 rounds. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 over four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0; handing the optimized interfaces unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite also beats DCI. The conclusions largely hold, but part of the BRIGHT gain comes from a strong retrieval ranking that one baseline lacks, which the main text does not make obvious; it gets its own discussion below.

1. The problem: one interface does not fit every collection

Recent agentic search methods all work within a fixed interface. RAG hands the model only the passages a retriever returns; DCI lets the agent read raw documents with terminal commands; DR-DCI first pulls documents into a workspace via dense retrieval and then browses them; RISE (restricted interaction-space retrieval) fences off a restricted workspace and adds model-generated tables of contents and section anchors to documents. Which of these wins depends on the collection: DR-DCI beats DCI on BrowseComp-Plus (73.1% vs 71.6%) but loses on BRIGHT (42.1 vs 45.7); RISE scores 65.0% on BrowseComp-Plus but only 25.9 on BRIGHT. The authors conclude that interfaces should be designed for a specific collection and model, and that this design work can be handed to a coding agent.

The idea follows prompt optimization such as DSPy and harness optimization such as Meta-Harness. The difference is the target: prompt optimizers change only text, Meta-Harness changes the orchestration code around a model, and SearchWeaver changes how the collection the agent faces is organized and which operations it can call.

2. Method: a coding agent repeatedly revises the interface

2.1 What an interface consists of

A candidate interface has three parts. First, pre-built files: before any question arrives, the whole collection is processed once, for example to build a "title to file path" index reused by every question. Second, executable tools: Python scripts that can call the supplied BM25 and dense retrieval, restrict search to a subdirectory, or combine the agent's document judgments with a retrieval ranking. Third, usage instructions telling the search agent when to use which tool and how to check clues. The three must be designed together: a tool that "merges the agent's judgments into the ranking" needs instructions telling the agent when to read documents and how to pass its judgments to the tool.

A candidate may also replace the search agent's base system prompt and its context-management policy (which decides when earlier tool outputs get truncated or cleared). The search agent's model weights never change.

2.2 The optimization loop

Each round, the designer looks at the collection and all previous candidates and writes a new interface; the new interface is run on the optimization questions, returning per-question scores and full execution logs, including which commands were run, what tools returned, and the final answer. Gold document IDs for optimization questions are also given to the designer, helping it distinguish "never found" from "found but not recognized". Every candidate's results are kept for later reference whether or not it improved. After 10 rounds, the interface with the highest mean score on the optimization set is evaluated on the test questions.

Leakage safeguards are in the appendix: a candidate whose files contain optimization question text, question IDs or gold labels is rejected before evaluation, and test question and label files are made unreadable during optimization. The search agent gets at most 300 turns and 30 minutes per question.

3. Results

BrowseComp-Plus asks multi-clue questions over a fixed web corpus, hereafter BCP (multi-clue QA benchmark), judged by GPT-4.1, with 30 questions for optimization and 800 for testing. BRIGHT is reasoning-intensive document retrieval; four subsets are used (biology, earth science, economics, robotics), with 213 optimization and 210 test questions in total, scored by nDCG@10. Each collection gets its own optimized interface.

3.1 Main results

MethodBCP accuracyBiologyEarthEconomicsRoboticsBRIGHT avg
DCI71.661.651.531.338.245.7
Agentic search (dense)62.658.251.434.635.745.0
Agentic search (BM25)47.548.841.630.235.439.0
RISE65.034.929.417.721.725.9
DR-DCI73.154.443.431.739.042.1
SearchWeaver78.474.664.638.342.455.0

SearchWeaver leads on both benchmarks and all four subsets. With 800 BCP test questions, 6.8 points is about 54 questions, a reliable gap. Each BRIGHT subset has only about 50 test questions, so a few points on one subset deserve caution, but the roughly 13-point gains on biology and earth science are far beyond that noise.

3.2 What each collection's interface learned

The appendix shows the final interface for each BRIGHT subset. All four share a skeleton: the agent still searches and reads raw files with the shell, and a final tool merges the agent's judgments with a ready-made dense ranking into the submitted list. They differ in where retrieval enters and how much weight the agent's judgments get. Biology confines search to the question's topic directory; the agent labels documents it reads as encyclopedia, paper or web, and a merging tool ranks the submitted 20 from three candidate sources: documents labeled encyclopedia, the dense ranking inside the directory, and files similar to the first encyclopedia document. The appendix gives only these three sources and that paper and web documents count at half weight, not the merging formula or each source's share; in its example, the two encyclopedia documents rank 1 and 2, and places 3 to 5 go to two web pages and another chunk from the same source. Earth science searches like plain DCI and uses retrieval only for the final ranking. Economics starts from dense candidates, keeps the agent's order and fills remaining slots from the dense ranking. Robotics puts documents the agent grades as answering the question first.

None of these strategies was written in by hand, and they all differ, which is exactly the paper's point that interfaces should be tailored per collection. But they share one thing: all four BRIGHT interfaces end up relying on the supplied ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-8B ranking. The DCI baseline has no dense retrieval at all, the "agentic search (dense)" baseline uses the smaller ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-4B, and DR-DCI uses BGE-large. The paper does not report what that 8B ranking scores on its own without the agent, so the 9.3-point BRIGHT gain cannot be split from the main text into interface design versus stronger retrieval resources.

3.3 Is changing the prompt enough?

The next comparison partly answers the question from Section 3.2. Two variants: first, the same loop but only the instructions may change, with no generated files or tools and no retrieval resources; second, SearchWeaver's final interface with its generated files, tools and corresponding instructions removed, without re-optimization.

MethodBCPBiologyEarthEconomicsRoboticsBRIGHT avg
DCI71.661.651.531.338.245.7
Prompt optimization only75.671.456.241.838.852.0
SearchWeaver78.474.664.638.342.455.0
Files and tools removed72.564.953.138.838.048.7

Changing only the prompt, with no retrieval resources at all, lifts the BRIGHT average from 45.7 to 52.0, about two thirds of the total gain. That means most of the benefit comes from "telling the agent how to search this collection", not from the extra ranking. Only the remaining 3 or so points need files, tools and retrieval resources, and they are concentrated in biology and earth science: removing files and tools costs those two subsets 9.7 and 11.5 points. Economics is slightly higher without them (38.8 vs 38.3), and prompt-only optimization scores best there (41.8). In other words, the toolset optimized for economics did not help; it was selected only because it had the highest mean on the optimization set, which shows that selecting over 10 rounds and a few dozen optimization questions brings in some noise.

3.4 Tool time

The paper stresses that SearchWeaver saves time over DCI: tool execution time per question (excluding model inference) falls from 42.4 s to 32.9 s on BCP and from 63.2 s to 36.6 s on BRIGHT. The appendix breaks it down by subset:

BRIGHT subsetDCI mean (s)SearchWeaver mean (s)DR-DCI mean (s)RISE mean (s)
Biology62.212.38.01.7
Earth science78.863.59.82.2
Economics43.326.310.11.9
Robotics66.640.717.21.7

The saving comes mainly from biology, because it restricts search to one topic directory; the earth-science interface keeps DCI's whole-corpus search and saves little. Compared with other methods SearchWeaver is not fast: DR-DCI and RISE use a fraction of its tool time. It trades more tool time than those two for higher scores, so the authors' claim that it sits on the Pareto frontier among the evaluated methods is accurate, but "saves time" holds only relative to DCI. Also, only tool execution time is counted, not model inference time, which in multi-turn interaction may well be the larger share; the paper does not report it.

3.5 Does it transfer to another model?

Handing the interfaces optimized with GPT-5.4-nano unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite gives 73.9% BCP accuracy (DCI 60.9%) and 58.8 mean BRIGHT nDCG@10 (DCI 50.7), above DCI on all four subsets, with BRIGHT tool time per question falling from 23.1 s to 15.5 s. Working without re-optimization means a good part of what was optimized belongs to the collection itself, not to tricks for one model. Note, though, that with Gemini, RISE and DR-DCI reach 69.1% and 69.6% on BCP, both more than 8 points above DCI; gaps between methods shift a lot with the model, so a ranking under one model should not be taken as settled.

4. Limitations

The limitation the authors state is that experiments use fixed collections; when documents are added or changed, when the pre-built index and the tools that depend on it need updating, and whether that can be done incrementally, is not studied.

There are several more. First, optimization cost is not reported. Every round has Claude Opus 5.5 read full execution logs and then reruns the search agent over the optimization set; the call volume and cost over 10 rounds are the numbers anyone adopting the method most needs. Second, BCP optimization uses only 30 questions, and the paper does not analyze overfitting to them; the test gains show there is no severe overfitting, but that may not hold for other collections. Third, retrieval resources on BRIGHT are unequal, as Section 3.2 explains. Fourth, each collection was optimized only once, with no report of variation across seeds or designer models.

5. Practical takeaways

For teams building QA agents over an internal knowledge base, this gives a process to copy: prepare a small batch of questions with gold answers, and have a coding agent read the execution logs and revise the prompt, generate index files and write search scripts. The ablation says the cheapest first step is prompt-only optimization: BCP accuracy goes from 71.6% to 75.6%, BRIGHT gets two thirds of the gain, and no extra retrieval resources are needed. If the collection has a clear directory structure or decent dense retrieval, then let the designer build tools that restrict search to relevant directories and combine the agent's judgments with the retrieval ranking. If the collection changes often, you will need to design how the generated index is maintained.

papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.authors: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Yichuan Li, Qian Q...
papers.summary: Move a large model to a different GPU or framework version, and the training recipe that used to be fastest often no longer is. The recipe settles how the model is split across GPUs, which low-level routines to use, and how GPU data transfers overlap with computation. ATTUNE lets an AI agent able to write code and run commands tune recipes, given a recipe that runs and a budget of GPU-hours; it tries things and analyses bottlenecks on its own. But the real point of the paper lies outside the agent, in a correctness gate run by fixed code the agent cannot change. The model, data, batch size and numeric precision are locked, and any change that would quietly alter what is being trained, such as dropping overflow tokens, is rejected before launch. After fine-tuning jobs for three models switched to the tuned recipes, training ran on average 1.7 times as fast as before, and up to 3.9 times.

deep_reading.content_html:
Before training a large model, engineers have to settle on a "training recipe": how the model is split across tens or hundreds of GPUs, how much computation to trade for memory when memory runs short, which low-level compute routines to use, and how data transfers between GPUs overlap with computation. Move the same model to a different GPU or framework version, and the recipe that used to be fastest often no longer is. Amazon built a system called ATTUNE that lets an AI agent able to write code and run commands tune recipes: give it a recipe that runs and a budget of GPU-hours, and it tries things, analyses bottlenecks and keeps going on its own, with no one watching. But the real point of the paper lies outside the agent: a "correctness gate" run by fixed code the agent cannot change, which rejects before launch any change that would quietly alter what is being trained. After Amazon's fine-tuning jobs for three in-house models switched to the tuned recipes, training ran on average 1.7 times as fast as before, and up to 3.9 times.

1. The problem: existing auto-tuners either cannot find the answer or "break" the training

A training recipe has many "levers" that can be adjusted. The most important is how the model is split: each layer's matrices can be cut up across several cards, different layers can be given to different cards that pass work along like a pipeline, or the data can be split so that several groups of cards each compute one share. There is more: when memory is short, whether to discard intermediate results and recompute them when needed (trading compute for memory); whether to park some data in CPU memory; which version of the attention routine to use.

Existing auto-tuners fall roughly into three kinds. The first picks from a pre-listed set of options using a formula that estimates performance. The second is "black-box" search, such as Bayesian optimisation: it does not understand how the system works, it just runs trial after trial and decides what to try next from the results, but each trial is expensive. The third is the recent kind of large-model tuner, such as OptiCo, which can read performance analyses but likewise only adjusts a fixed list of knobs.

Two observations by the authors shaped ATTUNE's design.

First, part of the speed a stock recipe leaves on the table is hidden in combinations of levers that only help when changed together, and part in levers that the fixed list does not include at all, such as switching to a different routine for distributing data among cards.

Second, some settings quietly change what is being trained, while training still finishes without errors. Two examples. In "mixture-of-experts" models, each input word is sent to a few "expert" sub-networks. A common speed-up parameter caps how many words each expert handles, and words over the cap are simply dropped and not trained on. Another parameter, judging by its name, only "sends gradients at lower precision", but in fact it also makes gradient accumulation low-precision. A tuner that only checks "does it run" would hand both settings over as "optimisations", and the trained model would differ from the original.

2. Method: the agent searches, fixed code judges

One tuning job is called a "campaign": one fixed model, one cluster, a fixed number of GPUs. Every candidate recipe trains exactly the same thing: model, data, length of each example, examples per step and numeric precision stay the same, and every run even reads the same data in the same order. Each trial runs a fixed number of steps; the first few are warm-up and not scored, and after that the score is the average number of words each GPU processes per second.

Speed measurements are noisy, so first one has to decide "how much faster counts as really faster". The original recipe runs at least 5 times on different machines to get its average speed and its standard deviation as a share of that average, σ. The noise band is the larger of 3% and 3σ; a new candidate must beat the current fastest by more than this band to replace it. That way a run that happened to be fast is not mistaken for a real improvement.

The agent uses only ordinary tools: reading and writing files (including the training framework's source code), running commands, and calling the cluster's interface. A written "tuning code of practice" sets it six rules; the three most important are:

  • before every launch, write down a hypothesis: which bottleneck to ease, why it should work, and how much faster it should be;
  • change only one lever at a time, or one set of splitting choices that must change together, so the result can be attributed;
  • before using a parameter, read its implementation in the framework source to see whether it quietly changes other parameters too, and record the code location in the ledger.

When the bottleneck is unclear, the agent runs a performance analysis: a fixed analysis program splits each training step's time into computation, data transfer between GPUs, work on the CPU side, and idle waiting, telling the agent where time is mainly being wasted.

Spending is policed by fixed code. An accounting script counts from the moment the cluster allocates machines until they are released, including failed runs and runs used for checks, and nothing launches if the budget is not enough. Re-running a failed recipe unchanged is also refused, forcing the agent to find the cause before changing it.

The correctness gate has two steps, and it is the heart of the system.

The first step happens before launch: compare all parameters and environment variables that finally take effect in the candidate and in the original recipe. Final values are compared because one parameter may quietly change others. Every change is looked up in a register that the agent cannot edit. Changes that alter what is trained (data, examples per step, optimiser, loss function, routing, numeric precision), or that trigger known software defects, are rejected outright. Changes that alter only "how it is computed" and not "what is computed", such as a different way of placing data on GPUs, are passed outright. Anything not in the register is passed on to the second step and written into the report for a person to review.

The second step happens after launch: compare the loss at the first training step, i.e. how wrong the model is on the first batch of data. At the first step the weights have just been loaded and not yet updated, so the candidate and the original face the same weights and the same batch, and their losses should be almost identical. Legitimate changes only cause tiny differences from a different order of computation, whereas weights that were loaded or split wrongly make the loss change several-fold. So the rule is that the first-step loss must be within 5% of the original's, and no loss in the whole trial may be infinite or invalid.

To make it truly unattended, the authors added several hooks around Claude Code: the agent cannot finish until the budget is spent or it has written down a reason to stop, with evidence; when it wants to ask a person something, it instead "takes the default and records the assumption"; unknown destructive commands are blocked. Every run is written into an append-only ledger, so the system can recover even after a crash. When a campaign ends, the agent writes down lessons, which go into the lesson library for next time after human review.

3. Result one: faster than the strongest public recipes

The authors first reproduced NVIDIA's four official benchmark recipes unchanged on their own cluster; three came within 2% of NVIDIA's published speed, showing that the starting point was fair. From those recipes ATTUNE gained another 7% to 26%, putting it 6% to 17% above NVIDIA's published figures. The authors then took four models not seen during development and tuned them starting from public recipes written by others.

ModelHardwareSpeed-up
Qwen3-30B-A3B8 H100s+9.9%
GPT-OSS-20B8 H100s+17.4%
Llama-3.1-70B64 H100s+26.4%
GLM-4.5128 B200s+33.9%
MiniMax-M264 B200s+164.2%
Llama-3.1-405B128 B200s+6.8%
Mixtral-8x22B128 H100s0% (original kept)

How much speed can be gained depends on how far the original recipe is from the current setting. MiniMax-M2's original recipe was written for reinforcement learning on 128 cards and kept the optimiser's data in CPU memory to save GPU memory; on 64 cards doing ordinary training, that trick slows things down instead. ATTUNE turned it off and changed how the pipeline was split, raising the speed to 2.6 times the original. GLM-4.5's recipe was written for H100s; on B200s the diagnosis found the bottleneck had become transferring data between machines and launching many small compute tasks. ATTUNE therefore shrank expert parallelism so that each expert group sits on the GPUs of one machine. Every token's experts are then local, and the data exchange between experts no longer crosses machines; the routing rule and the model are unchanged, only the placement of experts on GPUs. The fastest campaign also cut tensor parallelism to 1. Llama-3.1-70B switched to a faster attention routine, and computation came to take 98.5% of each step, with almost no idle waiting. The Mixtral and 405B recipes had already been tuned by the vendor for the same hardware, leaving little to gain; Mixtral's best candidate stayed within the noise, so by the rules the original recipe was kept.

4. Result two: with the same budget, it finds better recipes than other tuners

The authors gave every tuning method the same budget: 30 times the GPU-hours of one trial of the original recipe, with the same gate and the same release rules, and 3 campaigns per model. On GLM-4.5, ATTUNE gained 33.9% on average using only 669 GPU-hours and 6.4 hours; OptiCo gained nothing yet spent 1,407 GPU-hours; random search gained 7.8%; Bayesian optimisation only 1.8%. On MiniMax-M2, ATTUNE gained 164.2%, the best rival 55.5%. This shows ATTUNE not only found faster recipes but also spent less on the tuning itself.

Most interesting is why OptiCo failed. The way of splitting the model that ATTUNE found on GLM-4.5 is actually within the 11 knobs OptiCo can adjust: rebuilt from those 11 knobs alone, it runs within 2% of ATTUNE's final recipe, but OptiCo did not find it: it only tried the relevant setting with shallower pipelines, and its data exchange between experts always crossed machines. The answer was inside the black-box search space, but without diagnosis to point the way, most attempts either ran out of memory or were slower than the current best and got discarded. This shows that ATTUNE's advantage comes mainly from "look at the bottleneck before acting", not merely from having more things it can change.

The authors also removed ATTUNE's parts one at a time to see the effect. Without the code of practice and lesson library, the speed-ups on the two test models fell from 88.0% to 66.9% and from 49.4% to 42.9%, and half the trials failed to launch properly. Allowed only OptiCo's 11 knobs, GLM-4.7-Flash got just 18.1%, because its biggest gain came from turning off "keep optimiser data in CPU memory", which is not on that list.

5. Can the gate itself be trusted

The authors tested the gate specifically. All 460 legitimate runs were passed, and every configuration error was rejected before launch. They then deliberately planted 6 kinds of errors in the code: the 2 that change the model's forward computation raised the first-step loss by over 150% and were caught. Errors that only act when weights are updated, such as leaving out part of the gradient summation, cannot be seen at the first step at all. Shifting the labels by one word when computing the loss changed it by only 2%, about the same as the largest legitimate difference. These slipped through.

The gate also proved its worth in real use. On Nemotron-3-Nano, the configuration check blocked 19 pipeline splits with "unequal numbers of layers per stage". One of them happened to be the fastest of all trials, but it loaded other layers' weights into the wrong layers, and its first-step loss was 215% to 768% higher than normal. Without the gate, this "fastest recipe" would have been handed over.

6. Limitations and practical meaning

The authors list three limitations. First, the gate only looks at the configuration and the first step, so errors that act only when weights are updated go unnoticed, and a full training run is still needed for validation before real use. Second, the lesson library comes from past tuning, and GLM-4.5 belongs to the same family as a model used during development, so some of the gain may come from "having seen something similar". Without the lesson library, however, GLM-4.5's result was within the noise of the full system. Third, ATTUNE only tunes configuration the framework exposes; it does not change low-level compute routines or code, and does not cover the part of reinforcement learning where the model generates samples. There is one more lesson: when the authors went back and checked the lesson library, about one fifth of the entries were wrong, some holding only for the job on which they were first measured.

For training-platform teams, the most useful parts to borrow are the gate and the accounting, not the agent itself. Whether tuning is done by a person or an agent, you can first build a set of checks: compare the parameters that finally take effect, look them up in an uneditable register of "changes that alter what is trained", then compare the first-step loss. That keeps parameters which quietly change training, like "drop words over the cap" or "accumulate gradients at low precision", out before launch. Budgets should count from machine allocation to release, failed runs included. If your recipe was carried over from other hardware or another task (such as reinforcement learning), auto-tuning pays off most; if you use a vendor recipe tuned for the same hardware, expect much less, as in the paper such recipes gained only 0% to 26%. The lesson library should be checked against the original records regularly, keeping only entries the model does not already know or that correct its wrong intuitions.

papers.title: RemoteANN: A Native Vector Search Engine for Cloud Object Storage
papers.authors: Yutong Gou, Silu Huang, Yue Wang, Jianjun Chen, Cheng Long
papers.summary: RemoteANN co-designs vector indexing and query execution for cloud object storage. Quantized inverted lists, reordered data, merged range reads and local SSD caching reduce remote I/O. At matched target recall, the authors report up to 5.9× higher throughput than representative baselines.
papers.key_insight: The useful optimization target is remote requests per query. Data locality makes request merging and caching effective; faster distance computation alone cannot remove object-store latency.

papers.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
papers.authors: Jing Wei, Guanyi Chen, Qi Chen, Chuyu Zhang, Zheng Zhou, Chutian Wang, Jian Zhang
papers.summary: When NVIDIA's GDS reads data from SSD straight into GPU memory, the authors measured that 99.6% of the time for asynchronous reads was stuck at the step of submitting requests. Large-model inference services store the KV cache they have already computed on SSDs, so that the next request with the same opening can read it back instead of recomputing, and the speed of this read feeds directly into time-to-first-token. uGDS moves the job of telling the SSD what to do out of the operating-system kernel and into an ordinary program. Data still goes straight from SSD to GPU; what changes is who gives the orders. uGDS's batched reads are up to 12 times as fast as GDS, and plugged into an open-source cache system, the median time-to-first-token for long prompts fell from 1.9 seconds to 0.7 seconds.

deep_reading.content_html:
Large-model inference services store the KV cache they have already computed on SSDs, so that the next request with the same opening can read them back instead of recomputing. NVIDIA provides GPU Direct Storage (GDS for short below) for this, letting data go from SSD straight into GPU memory without a stop in host memory. Yet when the authors measured it inside the open-source cache system LMCache, asynchronous reads through GDS on a single task queue reached only 2.36 GiB/s, less than half of synchronous read bandwidth; 99.6% of the time was stuck at the "submit request" step. This paper from Sun Yat-sen University, HKUST (Guangzhou) and others open-sources uGDS, which moves the job of "telling the SSD what to do" out of the operating-system kernel and into an ordinary program. Data still goes straight from SSD to GPU; what changes is who gives the orders. On one A100 GPU plus one Samsung 990 PRO SSD, uGDS's batched reads are up to 12 times as fast as GDS and batched writes up to 30 times; plugged into LMCache, the median time-to-first-token for long prompts (from sending a request to seeing the first output word) fell from 1.9 seconds to 0.7 seconds.

1. The problem: data no longer takes a detour, but commands still do

First, the difference between the "data path" and the "control path". The data path is where the data itself flows from and to; the control path is who tells the hardware, and through which steps, "move this piece of data to that place".

GDS fixed the data path: an SSD can DMA data over PCIe straight into GPU memory, without the CPU copying it. But GDS's control path enters the operating-system kernel every time: a read request passes in turn through the virtual file system, the actual file system, the block-device layer and the kernel's SSD driver, and NVIDIA's kernel module also looks up a GPU address for every 4 KiB page of data. When moving one large block, these fixed costs are spread thin and hardly noticed; but in KV cache reads and writes and vector search, requests tend to be small, frequent and latency-sensitive, and these costs become the main expense.

The authors point to two further problems with GDS.

First, the queueing rules are too rigid. GDS's asynchronous interface inherits the rule of GPU task queues (CUDA streams): within one queue, every request waits for the previous one to finish. But when LMCache reads back a stretch of cache, the small pieces need no particular order; they only have to all arrive before the model's computation begins. To use the full bandwidth, applications have to spread requests over many queues, effectively doing GDS's scheduling for it.

Second, problems are invisible. GDS's kernel part is open source, but the user-space library that handles batched submission, background threads and queue integration is released only as a binary. When things stall you can neither find the cause nor change the policy.

Others had already driven SSDs directly from ordinary programs, showing that this path works, but those prototypes supported only NVIDIA GPUs, assumed a single submitting thread, and did not track "requests still in flight", so a program could free a piece of GPU memory while the SSD was still writing into it.

2. Method: the CPU gives commands, the SSD moves data, the GPU only computes

uGDS separates three things.

At start-up, privileged setup is done once, by a small kernel module: it takes the SSD over from the kernel driver, maps the SSD's control registers and command queues into memory the program can read and write directly, locks the GPU memory to be used, and records its addresses on the bus.

During normal reads and writes the kernel is not involved at all. Following the SSD's protocol (NVMe, the standard command format for solid-state drives), the program itself writes a 64-byte command saying where on the disk to read, how much, and which pages of GPU memory to put it in. It then writes a number into a "doorbell" register on the SSD to signal a new command. After that it checks the completion queue for the SSD's report that it is done. The whole process is ordinary memory reads and writes, with no system calls.

The data itself still moves directly between the SSD and GPU memory, not through host memory.

The cost is that the SSD must be detached from the kernel driver and given to uGDS exclusively, and the program sees "byte number such-and-such on the disk" rather than files. The authors argue this fits cache engines like LMCache and Mooncake, which manage their own storage blocks; if files are needed, a user-space file system can be layered on top.

To make this path both fast and safe, uGDS has four designs.

First, it supports both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. When GPU memory is registered, each vendor's memory addresses are translated into a uniform list of page addresses the SSD understands, so code above does not need to know whose card it is.

Second, command queues are split into two groups. SSDs support several sets of command queues. uGDS sets aside one deep queue just for batched requests, and the rest serve single synchronous requests. That way, when a large batch floods in, single requests are not left waiting behind it. Batched requests also gather many commands and ring the "doorbell" only once, saving repeated notification costs.

Third, it prevents "freeing while writing". This is where driving hardware yourself most easily goes wrong. For each request sent, uGDS notes "transfer in flight" against the GPU memory involved; trying to free that memory while a transfer is in flight is refused outright. Each registration also carries an increasing number, so that an old request cannot hit newly allocated memory that reuses the same address. If a command times out, the disk is marked faulty and isolated, and resources can only be reclaimed after a hardware reset confirms the SSD has stopped.

Fourth, completion notification is selectable. By default the CPU keeps polling the completion queue, which responds fastest but occupies a whole CPU core. Hardware interrupts can be used instead, with the kernel only waking the program and everything else still done in user space.

None of these ideas is new on its own: SPDK, which drives SSDs directly from ordinary programs, has long existed. uGDS's contribution is turning them into a GPU storage library that maps one-to-one onto GDS's interface and can be swapped in for production use: it has synchronous, batched and queue-ordered asynchronous interfaces, both vendors' GPUs share one abstraction, the safety mechanisms are in place, and everything from the kernel module to user space is open source. The most practical point is that a single queue can use the full bandwidth, so applications no longer need to split requests over a dozen queues.

3. Experiments: small requests, batched requests and the first batch

Tests used a server with two Intel Xeon CPUs, one A100 GPU and one Samsung 990 PRO 1TB SSD, compared against NVIDIA's current version of GDS.

uGDS starts faster: median initialisation is 42 milliseconds, against 115 for GDS, which spends almost all of it opening NVIDIA's driver session, loading configuration and probing the bus topology. For elastic services that frequently start and retire worker processes, this saves a fair amount of time.

Single small requests gain the most. With 2 threads writing 4 KiB blocks, uGDS's bandwidth is 6.2 times GDS's and average latency falls from 48 microseconds to 7.7, because each request skips a long chain of kernel steps. With more threads and bigger requests, the bottleneck moves to the SSD and the bus themselves, and the gap narrows to 1.2 to 1.4 times. On an AMD platform, against AMD's equivalent library, it is also about 1.2 times as fast.

Batched requests lead across the board. The authors tested 36 combinations of "request size × requests per batch", and uGDS won all of them: reads 2.1 to 12.1 times GDS, writes 2.3 to 30.7 times. The smaller the requests and the more per batch, the bigger the gap.

Following an anomaly, the authors tracked down a problem in GDS. More requests per batch should mean faster, yet for 128 KiB writes GDS got slower as batches grew. The cause is the first batch: with 128 requests per batch, GDS's first batch takes 91 milliseconds to read and 118 to write, nearly ninety percent of the whole 64 MiB transfer time. This is because GDS defers mapping GPU memory addresses until the first read or write, and the authors suspect it also allocates the internal state needed for batching only at the first submission. uGDS does all this during initialisation, so its first batch is almost as fast as later ones. Even leaving out the first batch and looking only at the steady state, with 4 KiB requests and 128 per batch, uGDS still reads 8.8 times and writes 23.8 times as fast as GDS.

Polling and interrupts each have their uses. For small 4 KiB requests, constant CPU polling cuts latency from 21 microseconds to 9, at the cost of a fully busy core. For large 1 MiB requests, switching to interrupts lowers the CPU use of the requesting thread from 100% to 4%, with only 5.5% more latency. So polling suits latency-sensitive cases, and interrupts are better value for large transfers.

4. Real-world effect: inside LMCache

The authors plugged uGDS into LMCache and ran end-to-end tests with the small Qwen3-0.6B model and the vLLM inference framework. To test the SSD path specifically, they turned off vLLM's own in-memory cache, so every cache hit had to be read back from the SSD.

MetricGDSuGDS
Median time-to-first-token, 32,768-token long prompt1915 ms715 ms
Throughput, 1,024-token short requests, 256 concurrentabout 19,000 tokens/s (tops out at 32 concurrent)50,000 tokens/s
Share of total time spent on "submit request"99.6%1.0%
Single-queue asynchronous read bandwidth2.36 GiB/s5.49 GiB/s

For prompts from 3,840 to 40,704 tokens, uGDS's time-to-first-token is consistently about four tenths of GDS's. The time for the GPU to place the read-back data into vLLM's memory is the same on both sides, which shows that all of the saving comes from the storage path. Another key difference is scaling: GDS tops out at around 32 concurrent requests, while uGDS keeps scaling to 256, with 2.6 times GDS's throughput.

5. Limitations

uGDS must have the whole SSD to itself: once detached from the kernel driver, the disk has no file system and cannot be used as an ordinary disk by other programs. Currently one uGDS instance drives only one local SSD; using several disks together and reaching remote SSDs over a network are still planned. Synchronous requests are assigned to command queues in turn and hold the queue until done, so a large request slows small ones on the same queue; the authors plan a load-aware scheduler. The experiments used only one consumer SSD and one A100, with the IOMMU (the hardware that checks addresses when devices access memory) turned off, and the end-to-end test used only a small 0.6B model. How it performs with data-centre SSDs, and with several GPUs sharing a bus switch chip, remains to be verified.

6. Practical meaning

If you work on tiered KV cache storage (GPU memory, host memory and SSD) or GPU vector search, and the SSD is a dedicated local disk, uGDS is worth trying as a replacement for GDS. Small, frequent reads on a single queue are exactly where GDS suffers most and uGDS gains most.

Before going live, confirm three things: whether the SSD can be dedicated and detached from the kernel driver; whether the layer above already manages its own storage-block allocation, as LMCache and Mooncake do; and whether the server's IOMMU settings allow the SSD and GPU to transfer directly. When deploying, pick the completion method by workload: CPU polling for latency-sensitive inference nodes, interrupts for throughput-oriented or CPU-constrained jobs.

Even without switching libraries, two of the paper's findings about GDS apply directly. First, GDS spends tens of extra milliseconds preparing the first time it reads or writes a piece of GPU memory, so after a service starts it should do one warm-up read or write for each "GPU memory and disk" pair. Second, GDS's single queue gets blocked on submission, so critical reads should be split across several queues in parallel.

papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
papers.summary: TokenGate trains an existing model to skip less useful tokens in later layers. Token-gated attention supplies a learning signal for token selection. Across the tested tasks, the authors report up to 11.3× faster time to first token without measured accuracy loss.
papers.key_insight: Token selection can be learned during lightweight adaptation instead of imposed as a fixed heuristic. This targets prefill latency and memory, with an adaptation step required before deployment.

papers.title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
papers.authors: Xinyu Lei, Hong Huang, Jiebin Zhang, Hongyu Li, Jinlong Song, Decheng Wu, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Sujian Li
papers.summary: Grouped weight quantization avoids an explicit codebook search by projecting onto a structured lattice. At each format’s largest feasible batch, decoding reaches 1.97 times BF16 throughput. This comparison includes the batch-size benefit of lower memory use.
papers.key_insight: Treat storage format and feasible batch size as coupled decisions. Arithmetic lattice projection reduces codebook search overhead, while memory savings create additional serving capacity.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong
papers.summary: Lafa adapts pretrained autoregressive models into blockwise continuous-flow language models. A single model proposes flow-based drafts and verifies them autoregressively, reaching 2.54 times autoregressive throughput at comparable quality.
papers.key_insight: Drafting and verification can share a model. Retaining autoregressive capability creates a verification path for parallel flow proposals without a separately maintained drafter.

papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
papers.authors: Xiuyi Qin
papers.summary: An independent researcher compares "add 2:4 sparsity" versus "drop one precision tier" on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B under matched storage bits (including sparse indices) and matched nominal compute tiers, with measurements on L40S, H100, and RTX PRO 6000. ==As long as a lower precision is still available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower==: 2:4 + INT8 costs the same storage as INT5. At the FP8 floor, a retrained 2:4 model served by vLLM on H100 raises prefill throughput 27% over dense FP8 with matched GSM8K; but ==during retraining perplexity recovers first while reasoning accuracy recovers much more slowly==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Since Ampere, NVIDIA GPUs have supported 2:4 sparsity: in a matrix multiplication, one operand keeps only two non-zeros in every four elements along the reduction axis, and the tensor cores nominally run twice as fast. It can be stacked with quantization, so the real deployment question is: from the current precision, should the next step be adding 2:4 or dropping to the next lower precision? This paper by an independent researcher compares the two on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, at "equal storage bits (with the sparsity position index counted)" and at "equal nominal compute tier". It covers all six GEMM operand families of a transformer layer that could be sparse (linear-layer weights and inputs, and attention queries, keys, values and probabilities), and times them on three GPU generations (L40S, H100, RTX PRO 6000), over 220,000 configurations in all. The conclusion is blunt: as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower. Only at the lowest precision the hardware supports (FP8 on Ada and Hopper) does 2:4 earn its place: on an H100, a 2:4 plus FP8 model served by vLLM gets 27% higher prefill throughput than dense FP8 with GSM8K accuracy on par. But that model was retrained on 13 billion tokens; one-shot pruned models are unusable.

1. The problem: hardware still supports it, software has given up

On one side, NVIDIA has kept sparse tensor cores in every GPU generation, and Blackwell added sparse FP4; on the other, in 2026 vLLM and LLM Compressor removed 2:4 support because too few people used it. A split this wide shows that a direct comparison on real hardware is missing.

Existing pruning-versus-quantization comparisons mostly compare at "nominal compression", mostly for weights, and do not time "add 2:4" against "drop one precision" on the same GPU. The author points out four things that are easy to miss. First, 2:4 stores a position index next to every kept value, so it costs more than half the bits of its dense counterpart. Second, both approaches promise twice the throughput, but the datasheet does not say how much each actually delivers. Third, most operands at inference time (activations, Q, K, V, attention probabilities) are computed on the fly and must be pruned and compressed before every GEMM, a cost invisible if you time only the GEMM. Fourth, the hardware fixes which operand can be sparse and along which axis, so whole-tensor statistics (such as kurtosis) miss what 2:4 actually removes.

2. How to compare fairly

The first yardstick is equal bits, for comparing memory savings. Each format is charged for every bit it stores per original element: values, indices and scales. 2:4 keeps half of the elements but adds a 1-bit index per original element, so it saves less than half of the bits. The result is that "2:4 on 2m-bit values" costs exactly as much as "dense (m+1)-bit": 2:4 with INT8 costs the same as dense INT5, 2:4 with INT4 the same as INT3, and 2:4 with FP16 costs more than FP8.

So at equal storage, the real choice is "drop half the elements and store each of the rest in $2m$ bits" versus "keep all elements at $m+1$ bits each".

The second yardstick is equal compute tier, for comparing speedups: pair formats by datasheet nominal throughput. The 2x tier is 2:4 with FP16 against dense FP8 or INT8; the 4x tier is 2:4 with FP8 against dense 4-bit floating point, which only Blackwell has.

Under both yardsticks, accuracy is operator-level relative error against an FP32 reference output. The author defines R as "error of the best 2:4 configuration" divided by "error of the best quantized configuration"; R below 1 means 2:4 is better. To favour neither side, each picks the best from an equal-effort menu: the 2:4 side tries three pruners: magnitude pruning, which drops the smallest weights; Wanda, which ranks weights by magnitude times the activation size of their input; and SparseGPT, which after pruning adjusts the remaining weights with second-order information from calibration data. The quantized side also tries three: plain round-to-nearest; GPTQ, which quantizes column by column and pushes the error onto columns not yet quantized; and AWQ, which scales up the weights of channels with large activations before quantizing, to protect them. Both sides calibrate on the same C4 data. Speed uses cuSPARSELt sparse GEMMs, and for operands computed on the fly both sides pay for online pruning or online quantization.

3. While a lower precision exists: dropping one step always wins

On accuracy, at equal bits 2:4 loses at every storage budget on both models. At the most generous budget (the dense side in an 8-bit format, which by the conversion above lets the kept 2:4 values use about 14 bits), the error gap is over an order of magnitude; it shrinks as bits fall but never flips, and the closest case still has R just above 1. At equal tiers it is clearer: in the 2x tier, 2:4 with FP16 has five to sixteen times the error of dense FP8, for all six operand families. Across all compute comparisons, the few cases 2:4 wins are against weak formats: MXFP4 (4-bit floating point where every 32 elements share one scale restricted to a power of two, a coarse scale) and INT8 with a single scale per row. Against FP8 and NVFP4 (also 4-bit floating point, but with an FP8 scale per 16 elements plus one per tensor, a much finer scale) it never wins.

Operator error is not model quality, so the author also ran whole-model tests on the 15 configurations closest to parity, the most favourable cases for 2:4. On GSM8K, 2:4 is never significantly better than quantization and is significantly worse 7 times. RULER is a long-context benchmark that tests finding and using given information in long text. Where 2:4 is significantly better than its quantized rival on perplexity or RULER, it is mostly on attention probabilities: keeping the top two of every four scores sharpens attention, which helps long-context retrieval and perplexity but never helps reasoning.

Measured speed is just as unfavourable to 2:4. The table gives "rival time divided by 2:4 time"; above 1 means 2:4 is faster (Llama-3.1-8B projections, median over 2K to 16K tokens):

W means the weights are sparse; X means the activations are sparse (online preprocessing counted on both sides). The first four columns are all below 1, which means that of two approaches promising the same nominal speed, dense lower precision delivers more in practice. On H100, 2:4 with FP16 runs at only 74% of dense FP8's speed.

Putting accuracy and speed together, as long as a lower dense precision is available, every 2:4 configuration falls in the grey region: some dense format is faster and several times more accurate. 2:4 reaches the frontier only at the far right, once stacked on top of the lowest precision.

How online pruning is implemented also matters. The author wrote a fused kernel that reads the input once and writes kept values and indices once, running near memory-copy bandwidth; cuSPARSELt's own prune-and-compress path and PyTorch's semi-structured conversion are several times slower and eat most of what the sparse GEMM saves. Attention probabilities P are even worse: after online pruning and compression, 2:4 runs at about half the dense speed, so P cannot be used as a standalone sparse operand.

4. Why it loses: the deleted energy cannot be won back

The reason is a simple asymmetry. Quantization keeps every value and only rounds it; each added bit halves the error. 2:4 deletes half the values outright; what is deleted is gone, and no number of bits on the remaining values brings it back. The author adds up the squares of the dropped values over all groups of four and divides by the sum of squares of the whole tensor, calling this the "2:4 energy loss". For i.i.d. Gaussian data it is 13.2%, independent of bits. On Gaussian data the 2:4 side's error stays at 36% to 37% across budgets, while the dense format of equal bits goes from 0.6% at INT8 to 27.4% at INT3. The two would cross only below 3 bits, a precision no dense tensor core supports.

Once the mask is fixed, dropped values carry only pruning error and kept values only quantization error. They sit on different elements, so their squared errors (error energies) add exactly; every error below means relative error energy, divided by the tensor's total sum of squares, and its square root is the relative error, so a 13.2% energy loss is about 36% relative error. The 2:4 side's error is "energy loss plus the error of quantizing the kept values to $2m$ bits", the dense side's is "the error of quantizing all values to $m+1$ bits", and the square root of their ratio is the predicted R. Every term is computed directly from the tensor, with no fitted parameters. Its rank correlation with measured R is 0.93, and it separates 2:4 wins from losses with an AUC of 0.95. But 2:4 wins at only 3% of points, so the criterion explains how big the gap is and why, not who wins a close call. For contrast, the whole-tensor kurtosis proposed in earlier work barely correlates with the outcome. What decides the contest is the local structure of the tensor along the hardware's grouping axis, not its overall distribution.

The analysis also predicts the effect of Hadamard rotation. Before low-bit quantization, tensors are often multiplied by a Hadamard matrix (an orthogonal matrix of ±1 entries, rescaled), which mixes each value with many others and spreads a few large outliers across many elements. Because of this spreading, the four elements in each group become more alike, so pruning two of them loses more energy; meanwhile the flattened outliers narrow the quantization range, so quantization error shrinks. Both effects work against 2:4. In measurements, rotation roughly doubles R for Q, K and linear-layer inputs, and the criterion predicts the direction of change at 87% of points. Most real deployments rotate, so the paper's unrotated results are actually optimistic for 2:4.

5. At the lowest precision: a real speedup, but only with retraining

At the FP8 or NVFP4 floor there is no lower dense format to switch to, so 2:4 can only be stacked on top, and at this point it has no rival. The author makes the linear-layer weights 2:4, keeps attention in BF16, and uses the base Llama-3.1-8B. Linear-layer GEMMs with 2:4 on FP8 run 1.3x to 1.7x faster, the first time in the paper that 2:4 really wins.

End-to-end vLLM results on one H100; the 2:4 model is Sparse-Llama (a 2:4 Llama retrained on 13 billion tokens):
