2:4 plus FP8 has 27% faster prefill than dense FP8, 18% and 16% faster decode at batch 1 and 64, and 28% less weight memory. The end-to-end gain is smaller than the GEMM-level 1.42x because attention and the other layers do not shrink. Serving the same weights with dense kernels removes the speedup, so the gain comes entirely from the sparse kernels. In BF16, vLLM's 2:4 path is no faster than dense, and slower at batch 1.

The GSM8K column needs care. With only 250 problems, at around 0.6 accuracy the standard error is about 3 points, so the gap between 0.568 and 0.612 is within noise, and the author also reports no significant difference. And the 2:4 model and the dense model have different training histories, so all one can say is "no worse", not "2:4 is more accurate".

The real cost is retraining. The table gives WikiText-2 perplexity and GSM8K accuracy (250 problems):

FloorDenseOne-shot 2:4Retrained 2:4 (13B tokens)Author's retraining (1B tokens)
BF166.31 / 0.600–8.13 / 0.6128.19 / 0.300
INT4 weights6.90 / 0.54018.61 / 0.0328.45 / 0.5808.53 / 0.292
FP86.36 / 0.55217.82 / 0.0288.19 / 0.6328.25 / 0.308

One-shot pruning is unusable on every floor: perplexity more than doubles and GSM8K drops to about 3%, which means the model has essentially lost its reasoning. The author's own distillation retraining from the dense model on 1 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens catches up with Sparse-Llama on perplexity (8.25 vs. 8.19) but gets only half its GSM8K (0.308 vs. 0.632).

Perplexity overstates how much retraining has recovered: perplexity is mostly back within the first 0.25 billion tokens while reasoning is far from back, and the perplexity curve gives no hint of how far there is to go. Judging whether a sparse model's retraining is done requires a reasoning task. Sparsifying only some layers does not avoid retraining either: picking linear layers one by one from the lowest predicted error upward until they make up half the linear-layer compute, and applying 2:4 to them, buys only 1.14x to 1.25x.

6. Blackwell's sparse FP4 is harder to use

Blackwell's sparse FP4 is not element-wise 2:4 but "pairwise 4:8": each group of eight elements is split into four adjacent pairs, and two of the pairs are kept. The author verified on an RTX PRO 6000 that element-wise masks give wrong results in this format. Its kernels run 1.4x faster than dense NVFP4, but keeping pairs discards more than keeping elements, because both elements of a pair must stay or go together and cannot each be chosen by size. On Gaussian data its energy loss is 20.8%, and after one-shot pruning perplexity reaches 108.83, five times that of element-wise 2:4.

Existing models do not help either. Sparse-Llama, trained for element-wise 2:4, cannot be converted directly; conversion discards a third of its trained weights and breaks the model. With the author's 1-billion-token retraining budget, GSM8K recovers only to 0.132, against 0.460 for dense NVFP4, so at this budget it is not usable.

7. Limits and practical takeaways

  • Only two 8B models. The Blackwell conclusion is limited by 1 billion tokens and one untuned retraining recipe; whether longer retraining recovers it is not tested.
  • The 4-bit integer weight floor (mainly for decode) is not timed, because vLLM removed the matching sparse kernels. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth, where 2:4 saves only bytes, which helps on some GPUs and hurts on others.
  • In the speed comparisons, sparse GEMMs get an exhaustive tuning search while the dense side uses the library's default heuristics, which favours 2:4, and 2:4 still loses.

If the hardware still offers a lower precision (e.g. BF16 to FP8 on H100), drop the precision first; do not add 2:4. If you already deploy in FP8, prefill throughput is the bottleneck, and a well-retrained 2:4 model is available, 2:4 can give a real 20–30% speedup, but vLLM mainline has removed support, so you will be maintaining your own branch. On Blackwell, there is no ready pairwise 4:8 model yet, and the cost and outcome of retraining your own are not assured. When evaluating any retrained sparse model, do not rely on perplexity alone.

papers.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
papers.authors: Tianyu Fu, Ruoxi Wang, Zihan Min, Zhongqi Ren, Zhihao Li, Tengxuan Liu, Shengxu Mu, Hanling Zhang, Yu Wang
papers.summary: When an agent goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns, it pays a recurring cost. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before, and reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. The authors work at a different layer: leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. A simple policy of keeping the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs beats the common approach of summarizing at the length limit, with a pass rate 1.7 percentage points higher on average across four agent benchmarks and 27.7% lower average cost.

deep_reading.content_html:
An agent working on a hard task often goes back and forth with tools such as search, web pages and code execution for hundreds of turns. On every turn the model re-reads the KV cache of everything that came before. The paper measures that reading this old cache accounts for 82.4% of total inference cost, far more than generating new tokens. The usual way to save money is to delete or summarize old messages, but any edit to earlier text invalidates all the cache after it, so everything from the edit point onward has to be recomputed. A Tsinghua team proposes working at a different layer: leave the text history untouched and drop only selected entries from the cache, while the remaining entries are reused as they are. They built an inference serving system for this, called AKV. Across three models and four agent benchmarks, a simple policy of "keep the cache of only the 12 most recent tool outputs" beats the common "summarize when the length limit is reached" approach, with a 1.7-point higher average score and 27.7% lower average cost.

1. The problem: recomputation is expensive, and cutting everything at once loses information

The longer an agent's conversation gets, the more trouble the cache causes. The first problem is cost: the cache keeps growing and is read on every turn, so storing and reading it is expensive. The second is accuracy: a model can only handle so much context reliably, and once the content taking part in computation goes past that range, quality drops noticeably.

The standard fix today is to edit the text, also called "context engineering": delete old messages or replace them with summaries. But an LLM's cache is computed in order, and each token's cache depends on everything before it. The earlier the edit, the longer the stretch that must be recomputed. So common agent frameworks wait until the length hits some limit and then summarize most of the history in one go, keeping only the last few turns, which keeps the number of recomputations low. Cutting everything at once like this easily throws away useful information from the middle turns too.

The authors start with a comparison. They run GPT-OSS-120B on the first 100 questions of BrowseComp-Plus (a QA benchmark that needs many rounds of search to answer), 4 attempts per question with at most 100 turns. Keeping only the 12 most recent tool outputs by deleting text every turn costs 1.85 times as much as doing nothing, because of repeated recomputation. Summarizing once at 48K tokens cuts cost by only about 7% and drops accuracy by 5 points. Dropping old tool outputs directly from the cache improves accuracy and cost at the same time.

2. Method: three operations on the cache

The authors first separate two lengths. One is how long the conversation is as text. The other is how much cache actually takes part in later computation, which the paper calls the "active cache". Text editing changes the first; cache editing changes only the second.

In this framing, the paper defines three operations:

  • Append: the normal case. Read in new tokens, attach their cache at the end, and increment the position index.
  • Drop: exclude specified cache entries from all later computation. The remaining entries stay exactly as they are, the text history is unchanged, and new tokens keep counting positions upward as usual.
  • Reposition: renumber the retained entries 0, 1, 2… in their original order, and number the next new token after them.

Why is the third operation needed? Dropping does not make the position indices smaller. The cache shrinks, but the index keeps climbing and will eventually exceed the largest position the model can handle. Repositioning pulls the indices back down. For models that use RoPE this step is cheap: to move an entry from position p to position q, rotate its key by the angle for q−p; the value stays the same and nothing is recomputed.

What gets dropped? The authors looked at the model's attention distribution and found two patterns: older content receives less attention, and at similar distances tool outputs receive less attention than the model's own reasoning. So the main policy is rolling drop of old tool outputs: keep all reasoning content and the 12 most recent tool outputs, and drop the cache of earlier tool outputs step by step.

3. The difficulty: the same text can have different caches

In a normal inference server, the same text prefix means the same cache, so caches can be reused by matching prefixes. Cache editing breaks this: the same text, reached through a different order of operations, yields a different cache.

Take the example in the figure. All three paths end with only B and C kept. But in ①, C was computed while A was still visible, so it carries A's influence. In ②, A had already been dropped when C was computed. In ③, there was no A before B even when B itself was computed. So C's cache differs across the three paths. The paper therefore describes a cache state by "the full sequence of operations applied since an empty cache": for a given model, that sequence uniquely determines the current cache. The inference server has to remember both the text history and the operation history to reuse cache correctly.

4. AKV: turning this into an inference service

AKV's interface is almost identical to a standard chat API. The client sends the full message list as usual, with one extra optional field that says "after message N, drop these entries and reposition here". The client does not need to know which caches the server still holds; each turn it just appends messages and operations as usual.

Inside the server there are three mechanisms.

The first is reuse. Inference servers usually do prefix caching with a radix tree, so requests with the same prefix share a segment of cache. AKV adds "drop" and "reposition" nodes to the tree and matches on both text and operations during lookup. That is why ① and ② in the figure can share the A–B segment, while each keeps its own copy of C because A was dropped at different times.

The second is reclamation. A cache entry can be freed only when no in-flight computation still needs it. For example, once both ① and ② have dropped A, A's cache can be freed without waiting for the requests to finish. When GPU memory is tight, the server first reclaims cache that has been dropped and only then cache from finished requests, because the latter is more likely to be needed next turn.

The third is recovery. Once cache has been evicted from GPU memory, it has to be recomputed the next time it is needed. But a normal recompute from scratch can only produce the cache of "nothing ever dropped", and replaying each operation step by step would take many passes. AKV instead splits the content to be recomputed, at each layer, into segments at the drop and reposition points. Each segment attends only to itself and to the cache that earlier segments still retained at that time, and all segments are computed in one pass. This way a single computation restores the exact state after the drops and repositions.

5. Results

The baselines are two "summarize at the limit" approaches. The "standard" approach uses each model's own higher limit (96K tokens for GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, 192K for MiroThinker-1.7-Mini). The "text editing" approach uses the same summarization but lowers the limit to 48K for all models. AKV uses rolling drop with "keep the 12 most recent tool outputs". There are four benchmarks: two multi-round search QA sets (BrowseComp-Plus, xbench-DeepSearch), the 103 text-only questions of GAIA, and SWE-bench Verified, which fixes bugs in real code repositories. Cost is priced on tokens actually read and generated. To avoid favoring their own method, the authors also charge every token touched by repositioning at the cache-read price, deliberately overestimating the cost of that step.

Average over the four benchmarks (score is pass rate %, cost is cents per task):

ModelStandardText editingAKV
MiniMax-M2.752.4 pts / 5.0 cents52.8 / 5.753.7 / 4.4
GPT-OSS-120B51.0 / 11.248.3 / 10.253.1 / 7.3
MiroThinker-1.7-Mini44.1 / 20.437.1 / 18.145.8 / 14.8

On all three models AKV has the highest average score, and its average cost is 27.7% lower than the standard approach and 21.9% lower than text editing. It does not win every cell, though: on MiniMax-M2.7, text editing scores higher on BrowseComp-Plus, and the standard approach is slightly higher on SWE-bench.

Why does accuracy improve? The authors break the results down by conversation length. Below 48K tokens the three approaches are about the same; between 48K and 96K, text editing is worst; above 96K, the standard approach is worst. These are exactly the points where each one triggers summarization, which shows that the lost points come from information thrown away by cutting everything at once. Rolling drop removes the oldest tool outputs a little at a time, so it avoids this problem.

On speed, the authors measure serving efficiency on SWE-bench with 8 A800 GPUs. At the highest concurrency each system can sustain, AKV's average latency is 1.36 times faster, the slowest 5% of requests are 1.51 times faster, and output throughput is 1.18 times that of the standard approach. The gap widens as concurrency goes up: the standard approach runs short of GPU memory and keeps evicting and recomputing cache, so at concurrency 16 the slowest 5% of requests wait 230 seconds, versus 31 seconds for AKV.

Several ablations are also useful. Dropping without repositioning scores 55.0 on BrowseComp-Plus; adding repositioning raises it to 62.0, because the agent can keep searching instead of hitting the position limit and being forced to stop. Dropping the cache of reasoning content, alone or together with tool outputs, is worse than dropping only tool outputs. The authors also tried letting the agent decide what to drop, and two models reached 61.0% and 64.0% on a subset of BrowseComp-Plus, which suggests the policy itself still has a lot of room to explore.

6. Limitations and practical value

The limitations the authors list: what to drop and when still needs more exploration; agents have not yet been trained specifically under this mechanism; and models with newer architectures such as linear attention are not supported. A few other points are worth noting. The main policy in the experiments is a fixed hand-written rule, and the best "how many to keep" may vary by task. Dropped content still leaves an indirect influence through cache computed afterwards. The authors see this as a strength, but it also means results depend on the order of operations, so debugging and reproduction require recording the full operation sequence.

For teams building agent platforms and inference services, the value of this paper is that it moves "context compression" from the text layer to the cache layer. Suppose your agent produces a lot of tool output, such as retrieval results, web pages or code execution output, and you currently control length by "summarize at the limit". First check on your own trajectories how much the model's attention to tool outputs differs from its attention to reasoning content. Then try "rolling drop of old tool outputs + repositioning", the most robust combination in the paper. The prerequisite for deployment is a serving layer that can tell operation histories apart: if the server reuses cache only by matching text prefixes, different drop times under the same text will be mixed up incorrectly. AKV is built on SGLang, the code is public, and a client needs to send only one extra field.

papers.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
papers.authors: Irene Tenison, Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Daniel Karl I. Weidele, Nima Dehmamy, Dan Gutfreund
papers.summary: The KV cache a large model keeps in GPU memory grows with the text, and one way to compress it is to make the vector stored for each word shorter, but most existing methods only save storage. They store short vectors, yet at compute time must first restore them to full length, so computation balloons. RACE finds a way to shorten vectors without restoring them. Position encoding rotates each pair of adjacent numbers in a vector together, so as long as whole pairs are kept, the short vector can still be rotated directly. The pairs kept are those where queries and keys have the largest sum of squares on a small batch of text, and that choice is written directly into the model weights. On Llama-3.2-3B, with vectors halved and an input of 256,000 tokens, overall throughput rises to 1.79 times and time-to-first-token falls 43.2%.

deep_reading.content_html:
When a large model processes long text, it has to keep the intermediate results left by every word it has read in GPU memory; this "memory" is called the KV cache. The longer the text, the bigger it gets, and at a few hundred thousand words it often takes more room than the model itself. There are three ways to compress it: store fewer words, lower the precision of each number, or make the vector stored for each word shorter. Methods for the third way exist, but most only save storage: they store short vectors, yet at compute time must first restore them to full length, so computation balloons, up to 22 times the original. This paper's RACE (RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression) finds a way to shorten vectors without restoring them: keep only whole pairs of the coordinates the model's position encoding uses, then write that choice directly into the model weights. That way storage, position encoding and attention computation all happen on the short vectors, with no change to the inference program. On Llama-3.2-3B, with vectors halved and an input of 256,000 tokens, total computation drops 47.8%, overall throughput rises to 1.79 times, and time-to-first-token falls 43.2%.

1. The problem: storage saved, computation not

First, some background knowledge. In the attention mechanism each word produces a "query" vector and a "key" vector; their dot product decides how much a word should attend to each earlier word. The KV cache stores the "key" and "value" vectors of every earlier word. The length of these vectors within each attention head is called the "head dimension", commonly 128. Cut the head dimension from 128 to 64 and the KV cache halves.

The difficulty is position encoding. Most models today use RoPE: every two adjacent numbers in a vector form a pair, which is rotated by an angle set by the word's position. The paper calls each such pair of coordinates a "rotation pair".

The problem is that if a general matrix is used to compress the key vector, the compression and the rotation cannot swap order: compressing then rotating gives a different result from rotating then compressing. And the model was trained with "rotate first". So EigenAttention and PALU (two methods that compress vectors with a matrix) have to restore the short vector to 128 dimensions before every computation, then rotate. Storage is saved, but computation gains an extra restoring step. By the paper's count, with storage halved, the computation to generate each new word is 11 times the original for EigenAttention and 22 times for PALU.

Two other existing approaches each miss a piece. Thin Keys needs no restoring, but compresses only key vectors and leaves value vectors alone, so the KV cache can only shrink to 75%. The concurrent RAP (a structured pruning method) also keeps whole rotation pairs, but decides which to keep by computing gradients, which needs back-propagation, and looks only at the key side.

2. Method: keep coordinates in pairs, choose them by "energy"

The authors state the goal clearly: find a way to shorten vectors so that the dot product of a short query and a short key comes as close as possible to that of the original long vectors, while the shortening can be done before rotation. Two principles follow. First, queries and keys must be shortened the same way, because a dot product multiplies the two vectors coordinate by coordinate and adds up, so the coordinates on both sides must line up. Second, choosing which coordinates to keep must look at both queries and keys, because what is being approximated is their product.

Which kind of shortening can be placed before rotation? The paper proves an exact condition. If the shortening simply picks out some coordinates and drops the rest, then it can swap order with rotation if and only if the coordinates picked are exactly a number of whole rotation pairs, in unchanged order. The reason is intuitive: the two coordinates of a pair mix with each other when rotated, so keeping only one loses the part the other mixed in. As long as pairs are kept whole, rotating the short vector by the original angles gives exactly the same result as "rotate everything, then pick coordinates".

Next, which pairs to keep. The authors run the model once over a small batch of general text, record how large the query and key values are on each rotation pair, and add up the squares of both sides as that pair's "energy". High energy means the pair contributes a lot to the dot product. To compress 128 dimensions to 64, keep the 32 pairs with the most energy. The authors prove that the error from dropping some pairs cannot exceed half the total energy of the dropped pairs. So choosing by energy exactly minimises this error bound. The authors also note that this is not the same as minimising the actual error; it is a practical criterion that needs only one forward pass and is very cheap to compute.

Value vectors are not rotated, so compressing them has no such restriction. The authors follow EigenAttention: from the same data, find the 64 directions in which value vectors vary most and keep only the components along them.

The last step "folds" these choices into the weights. Picking coordinates and finding directions both amount to multiplying by a fixed matrix, which can be multiplied in advance into the weight matrices that produce queries, keys and values, and into the final output matrix. The result is an ordinary attention layer whose head dimension has gone from 128 to 64. Position encoding is applied only to the kept rotation pairs, each still with its original rotation speed. The dot products and weighted sums that follow are all computed in 64 dimensions, and standard PyTorch attention runs it with no specially written low-level code.

When compression is aggressive, an optional "recovery training" step can follow: using 1 million tokens of general text, the compressed model learns to imitate the original model's outputs, updating only the changed attention weights and leaving everything else fixed. At 75% kept this step helps little; at 50% kept it recovers most of the lost quality.

The paper's core contribution is spelling out "which compressions are legal". Once it is proven that only the "keep pairs whole" family can work directly on short vectors, the question changes from "how to restore" to "which of the legal rotation pairs to pick". The compressed model is just a standard model with a smaller head dimension, and existing inference frameworks need no changes at all.

3. Experiment one: can quality keep up with methods that restore

On three models, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Granite-4.1-3B, the authors compare RACE with PALU, EigenAttention, Thin Keys and RAP. Three measures are used: language-modelling ability (perplexity; lower means the model predicts the next word better), average accuracy on 15 common-sense tasks tested directly without extra training, and the average score on 16 long-text tasks (LongBench).

At 75% kept, RACE retains 96.5% to 98.5% of the original model's common-sense accuracy. At every compression level, RACE's common-sense and long-text scores are close to PALU's, without restoring at compute time; it beats RAP at every level and has the lowest perplexity at 50% and 75% kept.

The table compares the five methods with the KV cache roughly halved. "Computation per generated word" is relative to the original model as 1:

MethodNeeds restoringKV cache keptComputation to read the promptComputation per generated word
EigenAttentionyes50%0.7511.42
PALUyes50%0.7521.92
Thin Keysno75%0.750.75
RAPno50%0.50.5
RACEno50%0.50.5

4. Experiment two: does the saved storage turn into real speed

Saving storage does not guarantee running faster, so the authors measured speed on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Prompt lengths were 64,000, 128,000 and 256,000 tokens, each producing 128 output tokens, averaged over 10 runs per setting.

The longer the prompt, the bigger the gain, because with longer text attention takes a larger share of total computation. At 256,000 tokens and 50% kept, reading the prompt became 1.76 times as fast, generating word by word 1.90 times as fast, and overall throughput 1.79 times. GPU memory fell only 28%, not by half, because memory also holds the model's parameters and other intermediate results, which are unaffected.

The authors also tried stacking RACE with other compression: first RACE keeping 75%, then H2O or SnapKV dropping half the words, or KIVI (a method that lowers the numeric precision of the KV cache) halving precision, leaving 37.5% in total. The loss after stacking was larger than with RACE alone, showing that the two compressions' effects do not simply stay separate. Of the three combinations, stacking with KIVI's lower precision lost least, with especially stable perplexity.

Three more findings are useful. First, the text used to compute "energy" need not resemble the downstream task: between general text and task data, most tasks' scores differ by less than 6%. Second, looking at both queries and keys really is better than looking at one side, with smaller approximation error and the lowest perplexity; and this way of choosing is cheap, with calibration taking just 2.7 seconds against 8.3 for a gradient-based choice. Third, the authors trained three small models of about 245 million parameters from scratch, with the same total dimension but different numbers and widths of heads. Under heavy compression, the model with fewer, wider heads held up best, because each head has more rotation pairs to choose from.

5. Limitations

The authors point out several themselves. Choosing by energy minimises an upper bound on the error, not the actual error. Compressing to 50% needs one round of recovery training, so it is not fully training-free. When stacked with word-dropping methods, the losses of the two compression stages amplify each other. The paper's proof covers only the "pick coordinates directly" family of shortening; to avoid restoring, it deliberately gives up more general compression matrices, and it does not discuss whether something better exists in a wider family. Speed was measured on only one 3-billion-parameter model, and gains are smaller for prompts shorter than 256,000 tokens; the paper gives no results for larger models or for architectures where several query heads share one set of keys and values.

6. Practical meaning

For long-text inference services, RACE's biggest advantage is easy deployment: the output is a standard model file with a smaller head dimension, frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang need no low-level changes, and it can be stacked with lower-precision methods such as KIVI. You can pilot it on your own model at 75% kept: compute energy on thirty-odd thousand tokens of general text, skip recovery training, and see how much long-text tasks drop. To compress to 50%, budget for a round of recovery training on the order of a million tokens. If you are designing a new pre-trained model and expect this kind of compression at deployment, a design with fewer heads, each wider, leaves more room for later compression.

papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Ku...
papers.summary: In long-context decoding, every generated token reads the whole KV cache from HBM, so the longer the context, the slower attention gets. Sparse attention reads only a small subset of tokens, but at 50× sparsity existing methods fall far short of dense attention. The idea of SSA is that high-scoring tokens are always kept, the remaining long tail is sampled by proxy score, and each sampled token is up-weighted by its probability of being sampled. The proxy score is a quick attention estimate from compressed keys. After softmax, all probabilities are multiplied by one common factor, and tokens that reach one are kept outright. The factor is chosen so that the number kept plus the scaled probabilities of the other tokens equals the budget exactly. The rest of the budget is sampled with replacement by that probability, a token drawn more than once counts once, and its weight is divided by its chance of being drawn at least once. At the same sparsity, on AIME 2025 with Qwen3.5-9B, SSA scores 59.8 versus 36.7 for PQCache.

deep_reading.content_html:
In long-context decoding, every generated token reads the whole KV cache from HBM, so the longer the context, the slower attention gets. Sparse attention reads only a small subset of tokens, but at 50× sparsity existing methods fall far short of dense attention: on RULER-HARD 32K with Llama-3.1-8B, dense attention scores 88.76 while PQCache-style top-k gets only 72.51. This paper proposes Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA). The idea is that high-scoring tokens are always kept, the remaining long tail is sampled by proxy score, and each sampled token is up-weighted by its probability of being sampled. At the same 50× sparsity, Llama-3.1-8B's score comes back to 83.67; on AIME 2025 with Qwen3.5-9B, SSA scores 59.8 versus 36.7 for PQCache. The authors also wrote dedicated CUDA kernels, and at 1M context decode attention is 2.96× faster than FlashInfer.

1. The problem: top-k drops the long tail, and uniform sampling wastes budget

With a budget of k tokens, existing methods allocate it in one of three ways. The first is retrieval only: Quest and PQCache pick the k tokens with the highest proxy scores, and Tactic does top-p. This works well when attention is concentrated on a few tokens. Once the distribution is more spread out, though, all attention mass outside the set is lost, and with even a slightly off proxy score, truly important tokens land just outside the boundary. The second is sampling only: MagicPig samples approximately with LSH and applies an importance correction, which covers more ground but has high variance at small budgets. The third is hybrid: vAttention keeps the top-k and samples uniformly from the remaining tokens. It beats the other two, but under aggressive sparsity it is still clearly behind dense attention.

The authors argue that the problem is the word "uniform". The tokens left outside the top-k have very uneven attention weights (softmax probabilities, summing to 1 over all tokens), and uniform sampling spends the same budget on tokens that contribute almost nothing. They first ran a small experiment: for the same budget, they compare the attention output of the sparse approximation with that of full attention and divide the L2​ norm of the difference by the norm of the full output, the relative L2​ error. Sampling by proxy score gives lower relative error than uniform sampling across budget splits and sparsity levels (figure below). This is the starting point for SSA.

2. Method: stratify, then sample, then correct by probability

Start with the basic form of sampling-based sparse attention. Let si​=q⊤ki​/d​ and wi​=exp(si​). If each token enters the set S with probability πi​, multiply it by 1/πi​:
o=∑i∈S​wi​/πi​∑i∈S​(wi​/πi​)vi​​
Intuitively, when a token that was unlikely to be sampled does get sampled, it has to speak for a large group of similar tokens that were not, so its weight is scaled up. SSA builds on this form in three steps.

First it decides which tokens are always kept. Apply softmax to the proxy scores s~i​ (in the experiments, PQCache's product-quantization scores) to get qi​, then find a λ such that ∑i​min{1,λqi​}=k. Every token with λqi​≥1 goes into the heavy set H and is kept directly. The remaining budget m=k−∣H∣ is left for sampling from the other tokens, the residual set R. This way the size of the heavy set needs no hand-tuning; the proxy distribution decides it. The sharper the distribution, the larger the heavy set.

Then it samples from the residual set. Renormalize qi​ over R to get pi​, draw m times with replacement, and deduplicate to get S. The probability that a residual token is drawn at least once is πi​=1−(1−pi​)m, while tokens in the heavy set have πi​=1.

Finally it computes exact attention scores ℓi​ only for H∪S, uses weights exp(ℓi​)/πi​, and takes the normalized weighted sum. Tokens drawn more than once are counted once, so the number of tokens actually read never exceeds k.

Here is an illustrative example (the numbers are hypothetical). The context is 1 million tokens, sparsity is 50×, and the budget is k=20,000. Suppose 8,000 tokens satisfy λqi​≥1; they are kept directly. The remaining 12,000 draws are made by pi​ over roughly 990,000 residual tokens. When a token with a very small pi​ is drawn, its 1/πi​ is large, and it stands for a large long tail of tokens that each score low but together still hold a fair amount of attention mass. Top-k throws this whole tail away, and uniform sampling spends most of its draws on tokens near zero.

The existing families of methods are all special cases of this framework: with only the heavy set, it is top-k or top-p; with an empty heavy set, it is pure sampling; with a uniform proposal, it is the vAttention-style hybrid.

The authors also prove an error bound that shows how the budget should be split. Let AR​ be the true attention mass in the residual set, let aˉi​=ai​/AR​ be token i's true attention weight renormalized within the residual set, and let ρ=maxi∈R​aˉi​/pi​ measure how far the proposal is from the true residual distribution (ρ≥1, with equality when they match). Theorem 2 says that with probability at least 1−δ, the output error ∥o−o∥2​ is of the order AR​ρ/m​, with deduplication adding only a constant factor. So keeping more heavy tokens lowers AR​, keeping more sampling budget raises m, and the two have to be traded off. And once the proxy score underestimates an important residual token, ρ grows and the error rises with it.

The framework does not depend on which approximate retrieval method is used. Any top-k method that produces proxy scores (PQCache, Quest and so on) can serve directly as SSA's proposal, and when the retrieval method improves, SSA improves with it.

3. Implementation: keeping sampling from slowing decode

Long-context decoding is bound by memory bandwidth, and what SSA saves is the traffic of reading KV. To run fast, the actual kernel does not use an adaptive λ; it fixes the fraction h of the budget given to the heavy set, and the authors report that this matches the theoretical version closely. A decode step has four stages. The first three scan the entire context, but read only a few bytes per token.

The first stage computes proxy scores. Each key is stored as a 16-byte PQ code (16 subspaces, 256 centroids), while an fp16 KV pair at head dimension 256 takes 1 KiB, so scanning the PQ codes is far cheaper than reading KV. The first 128 tokens (sink tokens, where models habitually park a lot of attention) and the latest 128 local tokens are always kept; their scores are masked out in the same kernel so they are not picked again, with no extra pass.

The second stage selects the heavy set with radix top-k: it counts how many tokens fall into each bucket of the score's bits, from the high bits down, and in a few passes finds the threshold for the k-th largest score without sorting a million scores. The returned indices are unsorted, because the estimator above does not depend on order.

The third stage samples the residual. Building a distribution and sampling over a million tokens directly is too slow, so the authors sample hierarchically. Each draw first picks a 1024-token chunk, then a 32-token sub-tile within it, and finally one token among those at most 32. A chunk is chosen with probability equal to the sum of its tokens' pi​; within the chosen chunk, a sub-tile is chosen by its share of the chunk's pi​, and a token by its share of the sub-tile's. Multiplying the three levels gives each token a final chance of exactly pi​, the same as drawing directly over all residual tokens. Several draws for the same query can hit the same token, so each query (one row of the attention matrix) gets its own hash table to remove duplicates, and each unique sample is reweighted by 1/πi​. πi​ is clamped from below at 10−4 to keep individual weights from blowing up, at the cost of a small bias. Random numbers come from a counter-based RNG, which keeps the kernel compatible with CUDA graphs.

The fourth stage gathers the selected K and V from the paged KV cache and computes attention with an online softmax: K and V are read in batches while a running maximum score and sum of exponentials are kept, the accumulated output is rescaled whenever the maximum changes, and one pass yields the normalized result without storing all scores first. To use more parallelism, each query head is split across several thread blocks, and the parts are merged with log-sum-exp. The number of splits matters: at 1M context and batch 1, 64 splits are 1.58–1.71× faster than 32. Going to 128 or 256 splits is slower, because launch and merge overhead outweighs the extra parallelism.

4. Experiments: the biggest gains are at aggressive sparsity, and proxy-score quality is still the bottleneck

There are three baselines: PQCache, vAttention (with PQ scores), and Oracle-top-k. Oracle-top-k computes exact scores before picking the top-k, so it cannot speed anything up; it serves only as a reference for "how good deterministic retrieval can get". All methods keep 128 sink tokens and 128 local tokens. The models are Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-4B/9B and Ministral-3-3B/8B, plus Qwen3.5-27B on LongBench.

Start with RULER-HARD at 50× sparsity. PQCache, vAttention (PQ) and SSA use the same PQ scores and the same budget and differ only in how the budget is split, so the gaps in the table below can be attributed directly to the allocation.

Note, though, that in the two 128K rows and in the Ministral-3-8B 32K row, Oracle-top-k is still higher than SSA. This shows the proxy score itself is not accurate enough, which is a ceiling SSA cannot get around. On the Qwen3.5 models every sparse method is within 2 points of dense, so there is little for SSA to win.

AIME 2025 requires generating 32K tokens of long reasoning, and here SSA's advantage grows with sparsity. Qwen3.5-9B scores 66.3 dense. At 50× sparsity SSA scores 59.8, while Oracle-top-k gets only 48.3 and PQCache 36.7. At 100× sparsity SSA still has 51.5, while vAttention (PQ) has dropped to 3.5. Conversely, at only 5× sparsity vAttention (PQ) is better, 65.4 to 61.0, so SSA's gains are concentrated in the aggressive-sparsity range.

The heavy fraction h is the share of the budget given to deterministic top-k, with the rest going to sampling. An ablation on the same AIME 2025 task at 10× and 20× sparsity shows that neither part can be dropped: with h between 0.2 and 0.8, scores are all 61.0–64.0. Giving the whole budget to sampling ($h=0$) yields only 40.2–42.5, and giving it all to top-k ($h=1$) yields 49.4–53.8.

LOFT and LongBench show no difference. On LOFT, SSA has the lowest attention error among non-oracle methods in every setting, but the task metric subspan-EM (an answer counts as correct if the gold answer appears as a substring of the output; maximum 1) differs by at most 0.04 across methods. On LongBench (Qwen3.5-27B), every sparse method is within 1 point of dense. In other words, lower error does not necessarily turn into a higher task score; it depends on how sensitive the task is to sparsity.

Speed is measured on a single H200 (16 query heads, 4 KV heads, head dimension 256, fp16 KV). With short contexts SSA is actually slower, because the fixed cost of the first three stages is not amortized: at batch 1 and 128K it runs at only 0.60–0.74× the speed of FlashInfer. The longer the context, the better the trade. At 1M, 50× sparsity is 1.79× faster, 20× is 1.39× faster, and 10× is only 1.07× faster. Larger batches give larger gains, reaching 2.96× at 1M, batch 16 and 50× sparsity.

Kernel optimization is why SSA beats dense even at batch 1. A reference implementation of the same algorithm without the optimizations from Section 3 runs at only 0.37–0.47× FlashInfer and catches up only at batch 8. The optimizations make it 2.95–3.80× faster. For sampling, the comparison is chunk-only routing: after choosing a 1024-token chunk, draw directly from its 1024 tokens without the 32-token sub-block level. Adding the sub-block level makes sampling 1.21–3.16× faster (the gap grows with the number of draws), and at 1M context with $h=0.4$ the sampling itself takes only 0.30–1.18 ms.

5. Limitations and practical value

There are several limitations. The actual kernel uses a fixed fraction h, and there is not yet an equally efficient implementation of adaptive allocation. Clamping πi​ introduces a small bias. Sampling is random, so decoding the same request twice does not give identical attention outputs, and reproducibility requires fixing the random seed. Below 128K at batch 1, SSA is slower than FlashInfer. In settings where sparsity barely costs anything to begin with, such as Qwen3.5 or LongBench, SSA has no clear advantage. As a next step, the authors want users to set the approximation error they can accept and have the system guarantee it, but the paper gives no concrete design.

For industry, the scenario where SSA fits is clear: decode services with million-token contexts, large batches, and sparsity pushed beyond 20–50×, such as session histories of long-horizon agents, very long document QA, and long reasoning-chain generation. If your system already has top-k retrieval such as PQCache or Quest, adding SSA is a small change. The retrieval index is reused as is; you only move part of the budget from top-k to sampling by proxy score and add the 1/πi​ correction. Before going live, sweep h on your own tasks. In the paper anything from 0.2 to 0.8 works well, while pure top-k and pure sampling are both clearly worse. If you only need 5–10× sparsity, existing top-k or vAttention is probably enough; SSA's gains are mainly in the more aggressive range.
